activity: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
knowledge_domain: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
fact: Brandenburg v. Ohio (1969) held that advocating force can be punished only if it is directed to inciting imminent lawless action and is likely to produce such action.
story:
The community centre smelled of chlorine from the pool downstairs and burnt coffee from the vending machine, and Aidan had claimed the folding table nearest the radiator because it was the only one that didn't wobble. He spread his binder across it: printed summaries, a photocopy of a case called Brandenburg v. Ohio, and his own handwritten outline, which at the moment said, in large letters, BOTH SIDES, and then nothing else.

"You look like a man preparing his own funeral," said Cora, dropping into the chair across from him. She was arguing the other case that night, the one about search and seizure, and she had the unfair advantage of already knowing which side she was on. The mock court had assigned Aidan something crueler. He would argue that an inflammatory speech was protected, then turn around, after a ten-minute recess, and argue it wasn't. Same case, same justices, same boy.

"It's not the arguing twice," Aidan said. "It's that I think one of them is wrong, and I don't know which."

Ms. Paquette, who ran the program and refereed from a metal chair with a clipboard, had explained the setup once, briskly, and refused to repeat it. The case involved a speaker at a rally who told an angry crowd that certain people deserved what was coming to them and that the crowd should make sure it came. Nothing violent had actually happened afterward, though two windows in the district got broken that same night by persons unknown. Murray was playing one of the justices and had already announced, with great ceremony, that he intended to be "a complete menace."

Aidan had started with the speech itself, reading it over until the words stopped being words. It was ugly. He felt a visceral dislike of the speaker, of the crowd, of the whole gymnasium where it had happened, and his first instinct was that a society ought to be able to throw that man in a cell and lose the key. Then he read the Brandenburg summary again, slowly, tracing the sentence with his finger the way his grandmother read hymns. Advocating force could be punished only if it was directed to inciting imminent lawless action and was likely to produce such action. He said it out loud in the empty craft room until it had a rhythm. Only if. Directed to inciting. Imminent. Likely to produce such action.

"That's the test," he told Cora at rehearsal, tapping the page so hard the table finally wobbled. "The Brandenburg test. Directed to inciting imminent lawless action, and likely to produce such action. Both parts. It has to be aimed at starting something right then, and it has to be likely to work."

"So which side are you on?"

"That's the thing. The speech is vague. Nothing about tonight, nothing about a place. But the crowd was angry, and the windows broke the same night. Maybe." He looked at her. "Maybe isn't likely. And 'what was coming to them' isn't 'go do this now.' But then I think about the two windows and my stomach does something."

"Your stomach isn't case law," said Cora, which was true, and also, Aidan suspected, not entirely.

The night of the mock court, the small gym filled with plastic chairs and parents and one toddler who applauded at random moments. Aidan stood at the folding podium in his grandfather's tie, which was too wide for the decade and possibly for the species, and argued first for the speaker. He walked the justices through the test, each element held up to the speech like a glass to a light. Not directed at a specific act. No imminence. No likelihood shown, only coincidence. Murray, being a menace, asked whether an angry crowd itself made violence likely, and Aidan said likelihood had to be shown, not assumed from mood, and heard his own voice come out steadier than he felt. Ten minutes later, on the other side, he argued that the speech was a match struck in a room full of fumes, that the crowd's anger made action likely, that the speaker had aimed his words at exactly that. He half believed it while he said it. He had surprised himself by meaning both halves, not performing either, and the sensation was not exactly comfortable.

The justices conferred. Murray delivered the verdict with the gravity of a man sentencing a ham sandwich: the speech failed the imminence requirement, and so the speaker walked, though Murray added, personally, that he hoped the speaker stepped on a Lego. Parents laughed; the toddler applauded; Aidan gathered his binder and felt something he could only call unfinished. He had won, or the speaker had, and he still didn't know if that was right. Cora found him by the vending machine afterward, and he told her, quietly, that the test was probably correct and that he still didn't like it, and that he couldn't tell anymore whether the feeling in his stomach was foreboding or the chlorine.

"That's called being eighteen," Ms. Paquette said, passing with her clipboard. She didn't stop. Murray appeared behind her, holding out his hand with terrible solemnity, and Aidan shook it.

activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
knowledge_domain: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
fact: The Taylor rule, proposed by economist John Taylor, says that when inflation rises one percentage point a central bank should raise its interest rate by more than one percentage point.
story:
Emile had promised Ms. Abdi he could run the economics club's stall at the Saturday farmers' market alone, mostly because saying it out loud had felt like proof he was ready for college in the fall. The table held jars of preserves his mother had made, a hand-lettered sign reading FUNDRAISER FOR ECONOMICS CLUB, and a tin for coins. His one customer in the first hour was a woman who bought apricot jam, paid in exact change, and did not ask what an economics club was.

Maddison arrived at ten with a thermos and the textbook they were supposed to be quizzing each other from, since Ms. Abdi had announced a test on monetary policy for Monday. She flipped to a chapter with a graph shaped like a shallow river and said, "Okay, inflation. Say it goes up one percentage point. What does the central bank do?"

Emile stacked jars so their labels all faced forward. "Raises the interest rate. One percentage point. You match it, you've cancelled it out."

"That's what I said to Rose-Marie," Maddison said, "and she laughed at me."

"She laughs at everything."

"Then explain why she's laughing."

Before he could answer, Rose-Marie herself appeared between a bread stand and a tower of cider boxes, holding a bag of apples she had clearly not paid for yet, since the vendor was chasing her with a card reader. She settled the debt, took a bite, and said, "Maddison's still wrong about the central bank, right? I heard him from the pickle stand."

Emile had read the chapter twice on the bus that morning, and something in it had snagged on him the way a thread snags on a nail. There was a name attached to the idea, a man's name, and a rule about how much the rate should move. He closed his eyes briefly, the way he did when retrieving something he half-knew. "Taylor," he said. "The Taylor rule. It says when inflation rises one percentage point, the central bank should raise the interest rate by more than one."

Rose-Marie pointed her apple at him. "Exactly. More than one. That's the whole point. If you only match it, you haven't really done anything."

Emile turned that over. Matching seemed fair to him, symmetrical, the way you'd return serve in tennis with the same force it came at you. Going further felt like overreaction, like shouting to answer a question asked at normal volume. But the book had been plain about it, and Rose-Marie was quoting it without the book, which meant she had understood it rather than memorized it, which was quietly humiliating. He said, "Okay, but why more?"

"You're asking why," Rose-Marie said. "That's better than Maddison, who just argued."

A retired man in a fishing vest had drifted over while they talked and was now pretending to examine the gooseberry jam. Emile, needing a sale the way a drowning man needs a plank, said, "Can I help you with anything? The apricot's good on toast."

"I was a banker for thirty years," the man said. "I was just enjoying the children's economics lesson."

The word children stung, and Emile felt the familiar pull toward saying something sharp. Instead he found himself asking, "Then can I try it on you? If inflation goes up one point, the bank should raise the rate by more than that. Taylor rule. Do I have it right?"

"You have it right," the man said, and picked up a jar of plum. "Whether you understand it is another matter."

"That's the part I'm working on," Emile admitted. "I know the rule but I couldn't defend it yet. Maddison thinks matching is enough, and honestly his version sounds more reasonable to me, and I can't yet say where it goes wrong."

Maddison had gone quiet, which for Maddison was a kind of concession, though he covered it by reorganizing the coin tin. Rose-Marie sat down on the curb and said, "He's being honest about it, at least. That's worth something. Half the kids in our class would just repeat the rule louder."

The retired man paid for the plum jam and then, instead of leaving, leaned on the table's edge. He asked Emile what he wanted to study, and Emile said economics, probably, and then heard himself add that he was starting to worry he liked the tidy parts of it, the rules with names, more than the parts that stayed uncertain. It was more than he had meant to say in front of Maddison and Rose-Marie, and he regretted it immediately, the way one regrets opening a window in February.

"You'll get past that," the man said, "or you won't. Either way the plum is excellent." He tucked the jar into his vest and walked toward the honey stand with the unhurried gait of a man who had nowhere to sequester himself on a Saturday morning.

By noon they had sold eleven jars and Ms. Abdi stopped by, counted the money without touching it, and said the stall had done its work. She asked how the studying had gone, and Emile told her the truth: he could state the Taylor rule, he understood that the rate had to rise by more than inflation rose, and he still could not fully explain why matching wasn't enough, though he no longer believed it was. She nodded as if this were a reasonable place for a person to stand.

After she left, Maddison bought the gooseberry jam he had been eyeing, his own small peace offering, and Rose-Marie divided her apples three ways without asking anyone first. Emile ate his slice slowly, watching a toddler across the aisle drop a peach twice before her father gave up and paid for it, the bruised fruit still perfectly edible, still sweet where it wasn't broken.

"One more question," Rose-Marie said, mouth full. "Real interest rate or nominal?"

Emile laughed, picked up the last jar of apricot, and said, "Ask me Monday."

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Canada's first food bank opened in Edmonton on January 16, 1981.
story:
The van arrived at Cedar Grove at ten, and Laura stood in the parking lot holding a clipboard she did not know how to use. Mr. Delgado, the activities coordinator, had told her the mobile food bank set up in the common room on the second Tuesday of every month, and that volunteers should arrive early, which she had, by forty minutes, because being late to her first shift seemed worse than being awkwardly early.

"You're the student," said a woman in a lanyard, already hauling boxes. "Taylor's inside. Taylor!" A boy from Laura's chemistry class appeared in the doorway, wearing a hairnet that flattened his curls like a defeated mushroom. "Don't," he said, before she could speak. "One word about the hairnet and I hide your backpack in the linen closet."

Inside, folding tables had been arranged into a rough horseshoe, and residents were already drifting in with their walkers and their shopping bags from 1987, it seemed, plaid ones with zippers that growled. Laura's job was the bread table: two loaves per person, or one loaf and a bag of buns, a rule that immediately fell apart when a small man named Pierre-Olivier argued that a bag of buns was, mathematically, several loaves. "Where is this written?" he demanded, tapping the cardboard sign. "Show me the statute." She gave him the buns and the loaf, and he patted her wrist and said she would go far in life, which she suspected was not true of everyone who caved that easily.

An hour in, a resident with a cardigan the color of oatmeal stopped at the bread table and frowned at the whole arrangement. "I remember when there weren't any of these," she said. "In Canada. Not one."

"Food banks?" Laura said. "They've been around forever, though. Haven't they?"

"Canada's first food bank opened in Edmonton on January 16, 1981," the woman said, with the flat certainty of someone reciting an anniversary. "I was thirty-four. My daughter was learning to skate. It's not forever. It's barely anything."

Laura said, "Oh," and then, because the line behind the woman was growing, "Would you like rye or multigrain?"

"Rye," the woman said. "The 1980s were a strange time to start needing something like this, and here we still are, needing it." She took her loaf and shuffled toward the canned fruit, and Laura stood there feeling the fact settle somewhere behind her ribs, the way a date does when it attaches itself to your own mother's age, your own grandmother's photograph.

At the break, she found Taylor stacking juice boxes and told him the date. "Eighty-one," he repeated. "That's like, my parents were kids. So the whole country just, what, managed without them before that?" He squinted at the ceiling. "That's either really good or really bad."

"Both, I think," Laura said. "It means it started because people needed it, which is bad, and it means people started it, which is good. I can't get it to be one thing."

"You're doing that thing," Taylor said, "where you hold two ideas until your face hurts."

"My face is fine," said Laura, and threw a juice box at him, which he caught, because he was annoyingly coordinated.

In the last hour a resident who never spoke, whom the nurses called Miss A., paused at the table and put one careful hand on a loaf of white bread without taking it. Laura, remembering her training session's one firm instruction, that the whole point was choice, that being handed a box stigmatized people in a way that shelves did not, stepped back and said, "Take your time. There's plenty." Miss A. stood there a full minute. Then she took the bread, and a bag of buns, and pointed at the raisin bread, and Laura put it in her bag too. Taylor watched from the juice table and gave Laura a small nod, like a co-conspirator.

On Thursday, Mr. Delgado caught her in the hallway before her shift ended and handed her an envelope. Inside, in blue pen, shaky but determined, was a note:

"Dear Bread Table Girl. This is Pierre-Olivier. I won the bun dispute. I wish to state for the record that I told my sister about it and she says I am impossible, which is not germane to anything, but she said it anyway. Also I have learned from my nurse that my tomatoes this year failed because of their genotype, whatever that is, and I blame the seeds and not myself. You are a fair judge. Come back Tuesday. The raisin bread goes fast. P.O."

Laura read it twice, then folded it and put it in her pocket, next to the sticky note where she'd written Edmonton, 1981, like a thing she intended to keep.

She was back at the bread table by nine-forty on Tuesday, hairnet on, sign rewritten to say two loaves or reasonable equivalent, pending appeal.

activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
knowledge_domain: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
fact: When muscle cells run low on oxygen, they convert pyruvate into lactate, which regenerates NAD+ so glycolysis can continue making 2 ATP per glucose.
story:
The mitochondria exhibit was on the second floor of the science museum, past the dinosaurs, in a room lit blue like the inside of a cell. Eva stood in front of a wall-sized diagram with her notebook open and nothing written in it. Tomorrow was the placement exam, and she had missed the entire unit on cellular respiration because of the flu, which meant she had one afternoon and a museum to disabuse her of the idea that she already knew any of it.

"The test is mostly this," Kash said, standing beside her with his hands in his pockets. "Glycolysis, the Krebs cycle, the electron transport chain. If you can trace glucose to ATP, you pass."

"I don't even know what ATP is."

"Energy currency. That's all you need."

Allie had drifted to the interactive screen where you could drag a glucose molecule through its steps, and she was failing at it loudly. "This thing is recalcitrant," she said, jabbing the screen. "It keeps spitting the pyruvate back out."

Eva moved over and watched the animation. Glucose split into two molecules of pyruvate, a small payout of ATP appeared, and then the pathway forked. If oxygen was present, the pyruvate went on toward the mitochondria. If oxygen was absent, the screen showed the pyruvate converting into something else, a word she copied down without understanding: lactate. Beside that branch, a counter read 2 ATP per glucose. She kept scrolling back to the fork and watching the two routes split again.

"Why would it do that," she said. "Make lactate. It looks like a dead end."

Kash leaned in. "It's what your legs do when you sprint. Coach talked about it at track once. When muscle cells run low on oxygen, they convert pyruvate into lactate."

"So it's just what happens when you can't do better."

"No, it's the point. My dad explained it after I cramped at the meet. The lactate regenerates NAD plus, and that lets glycolysis keep going. You still only get 2 ATP per glucose, which is nothing, but it's 2 ATP you wouldn't have."

Eva wrote that down too, then underlined it. "So the burn is a trade. You buy a little energy with a debt."

"That's a dramatic way to say it," Allie said from the screen, where she had finally gotten the pyruvate through.

Ms. Ricci, who had been standing at the far wall with the clipboard, came over on her slow circuit of the room. She looked at Eva's page for a moment, not touching it. "Don't memorize the fork," she said. "Memorize why the fork exists." Then she moved on toward the light exhibit, and Eva thought that was the most useless advice she'd been given all week, because the why was exactly the part no diagram showed.

She went back to the interactive screen and ran the oxygen-free branch four more times. Each time, the lactate accumulated in a little side pool and the glycolysis loop turned over, ticking out its 2 ATP per glucose, and each time she watched longer before resetting it. It was, she decided, both failure and rescue at once, which was not a category her notes had room for. She wrote "inefficient but alive" in the margin, then crossed out "alive" as too much.

"Closing in twenty minutes," the guard said from the doorway.

They took the stairs to the ground floor, and Eva, who had wanted the last look at the gift shop, ran ahead of Kash and Allie down two flights. Somewhere on the first landing her thighs went heavy, that familiar acid heat climbing up from her knees, and she slowed to a walk with her hand on the rail, breathing through her mouth.

"Two ATP per glucose," Kash called down from behind her, not even slightly winded. "It's happening right now."

She waited for him at the bottom, flexing her fingers against the ache in her legs. "You're the one who cramped at the meet," she said.

"I stretch now." He held the door for her. Outside, the bus was already pulling away from the curb, and Allie broke into a run after it, arms up, and made it, and Eva stood watching her go, then turned back toward the museum's locked front doors to wait for the next one, forty minutes, in the dark.

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: Under the US Help America Vote Act of 2002, a voter whose eligibility is in question can cast a provisional ballot, which counts only once officials confirm eligibility.
story:
The clock above Mr. Sánchez's whiteboard read 9:47, and Mason had been eighteen for less than fourteen hours. Around him the government class argued about turnout, about whether a single vote mattered, and Mr. Sánchez let them run with it the way he always did, leaning against the radiator with a mannerism Mason had learned to read over two semesters: arms folded, chin lowered, the posture of a man collecting evidence. "Don't historicize your own frustration," Mr. Sánchez said when Tom claimed the whole system was rigged. "People have said that in every decade. Ask what's actually in front of you." Mason wrote it in his notebook, not because he needed it for the test, but because today was Election Day, and today his own name was, for the first time, supposed to be on a list somewhere.

He had registered in September, the third week of school, filling out the form at the library table while Marion quizzed him on the counties for their map quiz. She had checked his spelling twice, because she was like that, and he had laughed and let her. His birthday fell eight days before the election, which meant the timing worked, barely, and he had thought about that sliver of luck more than he admitted. His parents voted early and without ceremony; his father went before work, his mother after, and neither of them had ever said anything about it at dinner. Mason wanted it to be different. He wanted the line, the booth, the sticker.

Flashback: he was nine, standing beside his mother in a church basement that smelled of coffee and floor wax, watching her disappear behind a canvas curtain. He remembered the sound the lever made, a heavy mechanical commitment, and the way she came out looking exactly the same and somehow older. When he asked her whom she voted for, she said that was private, and he had understood, even then, that privacy was part of the power of it.

After seventh period he walked with Tom to the community hall three blocks from school. The line was short at four o'clock, the retirees having come and gone, and Mason felt the nascent importance of the moment flatten out into ordinary fluorescent lighting and a folding table with three poll workers behind it. The woman found her place in the binder, ran her finger down the column, and paused. She ran it again. "I'm not finding you," she said, and Mason's stomach dropped as though he'd missed a stair.

"I registered," he said. "In September. At the library." He gave his address, his birthday, his middle name. Tom, behind him, said nothing, which was worse than joking. The woman checked a second binder, then a printed supplement, while a man at the end of the table watched over her shoulder. "There's no Mason Deloatch here," she said finally. "You can cast a provisional ballot. It gets counted once the county confirms you're eligible." Mason stared at the manila envelope she held up, at the word provisional, which sounded like an apology in advance.

He thought of Mr. Sánchez's classroom, the radiator, the instruction not to treat his own frustration as history. He thought about how the form had felt so official, the pen, Marion checking his spelling. Something was wrong, and he could either walk out furious or take the envelope and make them verify him, make the system do the work it claimed to do. "Okay," he said. "How does it work?" She explained the affidavit, the signature, the sealed envelope, the days it would take. He filled everything out at a table meant for the voting machines, printing his information in the careful block letters of someone signing something that mattered.

It was Marion, arriving to vote with her mother, who found the problem. She was studying machine design at the state college an hour away and had a habit of noticing details other people surrendered to. When Mason told her what happened, she asked to see his confirmation text from September, the one the county had sent, and read it with her brow lowered. "Mason," she said. "This address. Fourteen Chilton Road. Is that you?" He looked. Fourteen Chilton Road was his grandmother's old house, the one his family had sold in June, the house where he'd spent weekends his whole childhood. His mother had filed a change of address for the whole household over the summer, mail forwarding, everything, and somewhere in that paperwork his nascent registration had been attached to an address that no longer existed, in a precinct he'd never voted in.

"The provisional ballot," Marion said slowly, "still counts if they confirm you." That was the whole point of it, he realized; the envelope in his hand wasn't a consolation prize but a second route to the same destination, one that assumed neither his guilt nor his innocence. He tried to hold both thoughts at once: that the system had lost him, and that the system had built a door for exactly this. He couldn't make them sit together cleanly, and he decided, standing under the fluorescent lights with the sealed envelope in his jacket, that he didn't have to.

The woman at the table handed him a sticker anyway, the small flag-shaped one, and he pressed it onto his shirt without taking off his coat. Tom held the door. Outside the sky had gone the color of a bruise over the parking lot, and Mason's phone buzzed with a text from his mother asking if he'd voted yet.

"Ask me in a week," he typed back, and hit send.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: Under the US Fair Labor Standards Act, non-exempt employees must be paid one and a half times their regular rate for hours worked beyond 40 in a workweek.
story:
Violet had always considered herself the most responsible person at Willowbrook Day Camp, more reliable than Dhruv, who showed up with sand in his shoes from the beach the night before, and certainly more reliable than Thierry, who once lost a seven-year-old for eleven minutes behind the canoe shed. Ms. Ho had given her the junior counselor job in June with a smile that Violet chose to read as admiration. She was sixteen, she had a lanyard, she had a whistle, and she was being paid eleven dollars an hour, which felt almost like being an adult.

When Ms. Ho asked for volunteers to cover extra sessions during the last week of July, Violet raised her hand before anyone else could breathe. She told herself she was helping. She also told herself she wanted the money for the used telephoto lens she'd been researching since March, and she was honest enough, some of the time, to notice those two motives sitting side by side like campers forced to share a bench.

She took Monday through Friday, full days, plus the Wednesday evening overnight and a Saturday festival shift. Dhruv took only two days. "You're going to burn out," he said, trailing her past the craft cabin, where glue and glitter had fused into a permanent geological layer on the picnic tables.

"I have stamina," Violet said. She believed this completely. She also believed she had slept fine on the gym floor during the overnight, though in truth she had lain awake cataloguing every mosquito sound until four in the morning, and by Friday she was pouring juice into a child's left shoe without noticing until the child pointed it out.

The paycheck came the following Tuesday in a thin envelope with her name typed on a label. Violet sat on the steps of the equipment shed to open it, Thierry and Dhruv on either side of her, comparing their own envelopes with the solemnity of men reading treaties. She counted her hours first. Forty-six. Then she looked at the breakdown and stopped.

Most of her hours showed eleven dollars. But six of them showed sixteen fifty. She counted again. She counted a third time, pressing her finger under each line like she was checking a map. "Why are these different?" she said, holding the stub out to Thierry, who leaned in and squinted.

"You went over forty," he said. "That's overtime. Hours beyond forty in a week get one and a half times your regular rate."

"One and a half times your regular rate," Violet repeated. She did the arithmetic in the dust with a stick, because it felt too important to do in her head. Six hours at time and a half. The extra money was real; it sat there in the total like a stone at the bottom of a clear stream.

Dhruv, who had read exactly one article about labor law after his cousin had a dispute at a bakery, began to proselytize on the subject of workers' rights, waving his own pitiful thirty-hour stub as evidence of his own discipline rather than his own caution. Thierry played the apologist for the camp, saying Ms. Ho probably hadn't chosen the schedule herself, the board had, or the parents had, or possibly the weather. Violet listened to both of them and found she agreed with neither entirely.

She walked to the office trailer. Ms. Ho was reordering first aid supplies, a clipboard sagacious on her arm, and she looked up without surprise, as though she had been expecting a visitor all afternoon. Violet laid the stub on the counter between the gauze and the sunscreen. "I just wanted to make sure this is right," she said. "I'm not complaining. I'm asking."

Ms. Ho turned the stub toward herself and studied it, then turned it back. "It's right," she said. "You worked more than anyone else, and the payroll software caught it before I did." She paused, capping a marker. "I should have warned you when you took the Saturday. I saw the hours adding up and I let you keep going because you made my week easier. That wasn't fair of me."

Violet had come in prepared to defend the camp against her own suspicion, or to defend herself against a clerical error, and she found herself instead standing in a quiet trailer where someone was apologizing to her. "It's more money than I expected," she said slowly. "That part is good. But I don't think I can do that many hours again. I poured juice in a shoe on Friday."

Ms. Ho laughed once, a real laugh, and wrote something on the clipboard. "Next summer, if you come back, we'll cap you at forty unless you ask." Violet folded the stub and put it in her pocket, where it made a small square shape against her hip all the way down the trailer steps. Dhruv and Thierry were still arguing by the shed, their voices carrying across the empty field, and she walked toward them with the whistle swinging on its lanyard, holding the folded paper out in front of her like evidence.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: A 1985 study by Thomas Gilovich, Robert Vallone and Amos Tversky concluded that basketball shooters' streaks were no more common than chance, calling the 'hot hand' a fallacy.
story:
Victor had three hits by the fifth inning, and by the sixth the dugout had rearranged itself around him. Jace moved his glove off the bench so Victor could sit in the shade. Somebody's younger brother fetched him water without being asked. When Victor peeled off his batting gloves, Jace leaned in close, sweat line dark on his cap.

"Fourth at bat, you're up with guys on," Jace said. "You're hot. I'm telling you, keep swinging."

The field had that late afternoon flatness to it, the infield dirt pale and raked, the outfield grass going long in patches where the mower couldn't reach. Victor had played on this diamond since he was nine, and it had never portended anything before. It was a field. It didn't know he had three hits.

He flied out to left on the first pitch. In the parking lot afterward, Elise was waiting by the chain-link with her backpack on one shoulder, holding her phone like evidence in a case she hadn't decided whether to file.

"You want to know something weird?" she said.

"I flied out."

"Before that. Three for three. Then an out. That's the whole thing, actually." She scrolled. "There was a study in 1985. Thomas Gilovich, Robert Vallone, Amos Tversky. They looked at basketball shooters, and the streaks were no more common than chance."

"So?"

"So the hot hand doesn't exist. They called it the hot hand fallacy."

Victor took the phone and read the names twice. "Basketball. We play baseball."

"Runs are runs. If a shooter making three in a row isn't more likely to make the fourth, a hitter probably isn't either. It's just what random looks like when it happens to you."

Mr. Liu, who kept the equipment shed and had watched approximately ten thousand games from the third-base side, was folding the tarp when they walked past. He said nothing, which was his way of saying plenty. Victor thought of him as a kind of affidavit for the park itself, a signed witness that whatever happened on the field had happened, whether anyone remembered it correctly or not.

The problem was that Jace hadn't dropped it. Tuesday's practice, he stood in at the plate and made Victor throw him fastballs until his arm ached, because, as he put it, Victor was the guy right now, and you rode the guy. Wednesday, the coach penciled Victor into the cleanup spot, and Jace clapped once, hard, like a verdict.

"You don't get it," Victor said, tightening a lace that didn't need tightening. "It's not a streak. It's a coin that came up heads a few times."

"It's you," Jace said. "You were seeing the ball. That's not a coin."

Victor didn't have an answer that fit in a dugout. The study was one way of seeing, and it was probably right, and it measured something real across thousands of shots. But it didn't measure what it felt like to stand in the box with his hands quiet and the ball arriving slowly, which was also real, or at least it had been for three at bats and then it wasn't. Maybe confidence was just a story you told a coin. Maybe the story was what made the hands quiet. He could hold both of those in his head at once, and what he couldn't do was prove either one, and he was honest enough with himself to stop pretending otherwise.

Friday, the last game of the season, obsolescent scoreboard bulbs flickering through the fifth, tie score, Jace on second with two outs. The cleanup spot came around. Victor dug in.

From second base, Jace clapped twice and pointed at him with two fingers, then pointed at the outfield, an order and a promise at once. The catcher smacked his mitt. The pitcher came set.

Victor let the first pitch go, low. He could hear Elise somewhere behind the fence, not cheering, just watching, keeping the count herself. He stepped out, touched the plate with his bat, and looked down at the dirt, at the marks of all the cleats that had stood where he was standing, every one of them certain of something.

He dug back in. The pitcher's arm rose.

"Fastball," Jace called, loud enough for the whole infield. "He can't beat you."

The ball was already on its way.

activity: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
knowledge_domain: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
fact: The first known mention of binary search in computing was by John Mauchly in 1946, in the Moore School Lectures, an early course on electronic computers.
story:
The projector in the lodge was broken again, so the coding club taped its timeline of algorithms to the wall with painter's tape, a long paper road running from "Babylonian square roots" to whatever Alec had scrawled at the far end. Abigail stood in front of it with her laptop under her arm and a marker she had no permission to use.

"Binary search goes back to the dictionary," Alec said. "People have been splitting books in half forever. It's basically ancient." He was the loudest kid at camp and the one who finished exercises first, which gave his wrongness a kind of authority.

"If it's so ancient, name a date," Ava said, arms folded. She and Abigail had been assigned the same final project: build a program that finds a name in a sorted list, then stand up Friday night and explain why one method beats the other. Ava wanted to do linear search, the plodding walk through every entry, because she thought it was honest. Abigail wanted binary search because Mr. Flores had said it would win on ten thousand names, and she wanted to win.

"It's older than sorting," Alec said, tapping the timeline. "Move it left."

She didn't move anything. Instead she sat at the back table, where the camp's one shelf of books held a water-stained volume about the early days of electronic computers, and looked up John Mauchly, because his name was on the wall under ENIAC and she liked the sound of it. She read the page twice. Then she read it aloud to no one, to make it stick.

"The first known mention of binary search in computing was by John Mauchly in 1946," she told Ava at dinner, "in the Moore School Lectures, an early course on electronic computers." Ava stabbed her pasta. "So it's not ancient," Ava said. "In computing, it's practically newborn."

"It's both," Abigail said, and heard how that sounded, so she stopped saying anything and pushed her tray toward the tray return.

Thursday night the demonstration still didn't work. Her code kept skipping the middle element, off by one, and Alec leaned over her shoulder in the lab, radiating the confidence of someone who had not written any code. "You're calculating the middle wrong," he said. She extruded the bug out of the loop one careful print statement at a time, watching the indices march down the screen: eight thousand, four thousand, two thousand, each guess halving the world that was left. When she finally ran it against a linear search on the full roster of every camper and counselor, the counts came back 13 guesses against 6,741, and Ava, who had bet a soda, slid the can across the table without being asked.

Friday the lodge was obstreperous, sixty kids waiting for the bonfire, and Mr. Flores clapped twice for order and gave them the floor. Abigail set up a guessing game with Ava: pick a number between one and a hundred, and Ava would say higher or lower. Ava picked, smugly, and Abigail called out fifty, then seventy-five, then sixty-two, then sixty-six, and had it in six tries while Alec, doing it Ava's way for contrast, counted one, two, three, four, all the way to fifty-nine. "That's linear search," Abigail said. "Great when you don't know the order. But the list is sorted, so I can cut it in half every time."

Then someone in the second row, a kid from the robotics cabin, said the idea must be older than computers, older than Mauchly, and Abigail felt the whole argument rising again in the warm room. She held up the water-stained book. "The first known mention of binary search in computing was by John Mauchly in 1946, in the Moore School Lectures, an early course on electronic computers," she said. "That's the earliest mention in computing we know about. Whether people were halving dictionaries before that, I honestly don't know. Maybe they were. The idea and the code aren't the same thing."

Alec stood up in the back, and the room went quiet the way it did when he stood up. She waited for him to fight. He walked to the paper timeline with his own marker, drew an arrow from "binary search" over to 1946, and wrote Mauchly's name above it in his terrible handwriting, then stood back like a connoisseur inspecting a print he had decided, on reflection, to buy.

Mr. Flores asked, from the doorway, whether she would say the sorted list was a precondition or a constraint. Abigail thought about Ava calling linear search honest, about the paper road on the wall, about the off-by-one that had eaten her whole evening. "Both," she said. "It's what makes the trick possible, and it's what you have to pay."

Ava cracked the soda she had lost, took one sip, and set it down in front of Abigail's laptop.

activity: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
knowledge_domain: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
fact: In his 1963 book The Making of the English Working Class, E. P. Thompson said he wanted to rescue ordinary workers from 'the enormous condescension of posterity'.
story:
The attic smelled of mothballs and cold ash, and Addison went up anyway, because her grandmother had said the boxes were up there and because the essay was due Monday and she still had nothing worth saying. The prompt asked for a story only she could tell. She had predicated her whole application on being interesting, and so far the interesting parts of her family belonged to other people: the uncle who raced motorcycles, the cousin who had almost been famous. What she knew of her own line was three generations of people who had never once appeared in a photograph before 1950.

The light through the attic window was crepuscular even at two in the afternoon, the glass filmed with sixty years of soot. She found the box with her grandmother's handwriting on the lid, FATHER, in pencil gone the color of weak tea. Inside were a lace collar, a brass thimble, and a folded sheet of paper so brittle it crackled when she opened it. It was a wage slip. James Whitlock, spinner, she read, and a number in shillings, and a date in 1888, and a note in another hand at the bottom: fined 2d for broken thread.

She carried it downstairs on flat palms, the way her mother carried pies. Her grandmother was shelling peas on the back step, her thumbs working in a rhythm she didn't seem to notice. "Do you know who James Whitlock is?" Addison asked, and her grandmother said, "My grandfather. Why would you know his name," and then, quieter, "Nobody knows his name."

"He worked in a mill."

"Everyone worked in the mill. That was the whole town." Her grandmother dropped a pod into the bowl between her feet. "He died before I was born. My mother talked about him maybe four times in her life. Once she said he could whistle whole operas, and once she said he came home grey, and I have never been able to make those two things into one person."

Adrien texted back within minutes when Addison sent him a photo of the wage slip: this is insane, do you know how many spinners there were, thousands, and not one of them is in any book you've ever read. She sat on the porch swing with her phone and the slip side by side, and the argument assembled itself in her head without her permission. She had spent a whole term in history class learning about inventors and acts of Parliament. James Whitlock had predicated nothing, invented nothing, passed no laws. He had been fined two pence for broken thread, and the thread he spun had gone into cloth that had gone into the world, and the ledger of that world had simply not thought to record him.

She walked to the library in town and found, on the open shelves, a fat paperback with a cracked spine. The Making of the English Working Class, 1963, by E. P. Thompson. She had pulled it down because the title matched the town her grandmother came from, and she stood in the aisle reading the preface while the radiator ticked. In his 1963 book The Making of the English Working Class, Thompson said he wanted to rescue ordinary workers from "the enormous condescension of posterity." She read the phrase three times. Then she read it aloud, very quietly, because it seemed to want a voice. Naila, who worked the returns desk, looked over. "What's condescending about us?"

"Nothing about us. About after. Later people looking back and deciding what mattered." She held up the book. "He wanted to save them from that. From being decided about."

The problem came when she got home and her grandmother, who had been thinking all afternoon in the way of old women shelling peas, produced a second paper from the drawer of the telephone table. "You should have both," she said. "My mother kept two things." This one was a Sunday school certificate, ornate, gilt-edged, James Whitlock's name in flourishing ink, and under his name, in a column headed Conduct, the word Excellent. Addison set the two documents on the kitchen table beside each other. The mill fined him for broken thread; the church commended him for excellent conduct. Both records were true, and each knew nothing of the other, and neither was the man who whistled operas and came home grey.

She sat with them until the kitchen went dim, and when her grandmother asked what she was going to write, Addison said, "I don't know yet. The sources don't agree because they weren't asking the same questions." She turned the wage slip over. On the back, faint, in pencil, someone had begun a sketch of a bird and never finished it. Her grandmother put her glasses on and leaned close. "Well," she said, and touched the unfinished wing with one finger.

activity: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
knowledge_domain: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
fact: Binary search needs to jump straight to the middle item, so it loses its advantage on a linked list, where reaching the middle means walking through the items one by one.
story:
The basement smelled of dryer sheets and cold pizza, and Bryan had dragged the good lamp down beside the ancient laptop so the three of them could see the screen without hunching. Loic set his notebook on a milk crate, opened to the page where he had written the numbers one through one hundred in careful columns. He was supposed to present on searching algorithms in Mr. De Vries's class on Friday, and he had decided, with the confidence of someone who had read exactly one article, that he would demonstrate binary search and declare it superior to everything else.

"You've got the wrong snacks," Susan said, nodding at the bag of plain chips. She went up the stairs two at a time and came back with a bowl of olives, good crackers, and a wedge of cheese she cut with what looked like her mother's cheese knife. Bryan called her epicurean tendencies a distraction, but he ate half the crackers himself while Loic drew circles around the number fifty.

"Okay, so watch," Loic said. "I'm thinking of a number between one and a hundred. You get seven guesses." Susan guessed fifty, then seventy-five, then sixty-three, and on the sixth try she landed on sixty-nine. Bryan clapped with cheese on his fingers. "That's binary search," Loic said. "Every guess cuts what's left in half. If I did it the other way, starting at one and checking every number, it's linear search, and you might need all hundred guesses. On sorted data, halving wins."

But the assignment wanted code, not a parlor trick, and that was where the evening began to destabilize his certainty. Bryan had a project already half-built: a music collection, a few thousand songs stored as a linked list, each record holding a pointer to the next one, because a video had told him linked lists were elegant, easy to grow, the vernacular of real programmers. Loic had said he could add binary search to it in twenty minutes and make the lookup instantly faster. He said it in front of Susan, which was a mistake, because Susan remembered things.

He wrote it at the coffee table while Susan read over his shoulder and pointed out a missing semicolon with the tip of the cheese knife. The logic was simple and beautiful. Find the middle. If the target is smaller, keep the left half; if larger, the right half. Repeat. He added a counter to print how many items the program actually touched, and then a linear version with the same counter, and he sat back and waited for the numbers to prove him right.

The numbers refused. Binary search touched almost as many records as the plain loop, sometimes more. He ran it again with the songs in a different order, then again, and Bryan leaned in so close his breath fogged the screen. "That can't be right," Loic said. "It should be seven comparisons, not hundreds." Susan asked the question he was avoiding: "How does the program get to the middle?" He traced his own code and saw it. The list had no way to jump anywhere. To find the middle record, his code had to walk from the first one, following pointer after pointer, one by one, every single time it halved the range. The whole advantage of jumping straight to the middle item disappeared, because on a linked list, reaching the middle means walking through the items one by one. It wasn't a bug. It was the structure itself.

"So the search is fine and the list is wrong," Susan said slowly. "Or the list is fine and you picked the wrong search." Loic wrote both sentences in his notebook, then drew a line between them. He thought of Mr. De Vries, who had a habit of answering questions with other questions, and for once was grateful. The halving trick wasn't a law of nature; it was a trade, and it only paid off when the data let you jump. Whether an array was worth losing the easy growth of the list, or whether the list was worth a slower search, depended on things he hadn't even asked yet: how often Bryan added songs, how often he looked them up.

He started rewriting the code before he had finished deciding, copying the song records into a plain array in memory, sorted by title, keeping Bryan's linked list for adding new songs at the front. A hybrid, half done, no guarantee. Bryan slid the bowl of olives closer to Loic's elbow without being asked, and Susan closed the notebook so it wouldn't get olive oil on it. "Run it," Bryan said, crumbs on his chin, finger already hovering over the enter key.

activity: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
knowledge_domain: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
fact: Behavioral interview questions, such as 'Tell me about a time when...', are built on the idea that past behavior is a good predictor of future behavior.
story:
Elijah had the job listing folded into quarters in his jacket pocket, though he already knew every word of it: Boreal Coffee, weekend counter help, must be available Saturdays, experience preferred but not required. The bus lurched around the corner by the hardware store, and he spread his hands on the seat in front of him to keep steady. The interview was at four. It was ten past three.

"You're going to look at the floor the whole time," Adriana said, leaning over the aisle from the seat behind. "You did it during your Spanish oral. You narrated the entire presentation to your shoes."

"My shoes were a good audience," Elijah said, and Adriana laughed, and Clementine, beside him, opened the notebook she had brought the way other people brought luck.

She had written questions on the left-hand pages and left the right sides blank for answers. "Tell me about a time you worked under pressure," she read.

"That's the kind they'll ask," she added, tapping the page. "They're behavioral questions. They're built on the idea that past behavior is a good predictor of future behavior." She said it matter-of-factly, the way she recited chemistry definitions, and then looked up. "So what's your past behavior?"

Elijah looked out the window instead. The boreal cold had come early that year; the trees along the road were bare by the second week of October, and the fields beyond them were the flat grey of unplowed stubble. "I've never had a job," he said. "That's the problem. There's no past."

"You have a past," Adriana said. "You have the greenhouse project."

The greenhouse project had been his father's idea, originally, which was the part Elijah never said out loud. His father had cleared the corner of the yard two springs ago and then, somewhere between the framing and the glazing, lost interest, and Elijah had inherited four half-built walls and a stack of lumber with no instructions. He had finished it himself over that whole summer, working out the vents, the shelving, the schedule for watering, learning by failing and failing again until the tomatoes came in heavy and cracked and, in the end, edible. He had been proud of it in a private way that felt strange to say aloud, which was exactly the problem with interviews.

"Tell me about a time you solved a problem without help," Clementine read.

"The vents stuck in July," Elijah said, still watching the window. "The temperature inside was killing the seedlings. I couldn't figure out why, so I took one apart, and the arm was bent, and I bent it back, and I checked the other five before they failed too."

"That's good," Adriana said, and she adjudicated his delivery the way she adjudicated everything, holding up one hand like a judge at a meet: eye contact, pass; clear answer, pass; mumbled ending, fail, do it again. He did it again. The bus passed the school, the church, the long low warehouse where his uncle had once worked. He was beginning to see that the greenhouse was not a story about a greenhouse; it was evidence. They were not asking who he was. They were asking who he had already been, on the theory that he would keep being that person behind their counter on Saturdays.

Here is what Elijah did not know. Adriana had applied to Boreal Coffee too, three days before he did, and had told no one, and had an interview at four thirty, half an hour after his. She watched the back of his head and weighed it. He needed this job; his mother had said the word "budget" at the kitchen table in that careful flat tone that meant worse than it sounded. But she had done the math on the bus fare, on the Saturdays, on the fact that there was one position posted. She let it sit inside her without deciding, the way you carry an unresolved chord, and she kept drilling him anyway, because that was also true of her past behavior: she helped.

They pulled up outside the plaza and the doors sighed open. Elijah stood, then stopped, one hand on the rail. "Come in with me," he said to both of them. "Not into the interview. Just to the door. If I turn around and you're there, I won't talk to the floor."

The café smelled of scorched milk and lemon cleaner, and behind the counter a woman in a green apron was stacking cups, and when she turned around Elijah recognized her before she recognized him: Ms. Li, who had been his neighbor on Delmore Street until he was nine, who had moved away and become, apparently, this. She recognized him a second later and something crossed her face, a quick recalculation, and he could not tell whether it was pleasure or its opposite.

"Elijah," she said. "Sit down. You first, I think."

She asked him about the greenhouse, because she had heard his mother talk about it years ago at a block party, and he told it again, the vents, the bent arm, the checking of all six before the rest could fail, and this time he looked at her the whole way through. At the end she wrote something down and asked him to wait outside while she brought in the next applicant, and he stood in the cold between the café and the pet store, and the door opened behind him, and Adriana came out smoothing her jacket, not quite meeting his eyes.

"I applied too," she said. "Three days before you."

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: A 2001 review titled 'Bad Is Stronger Than Good', led by Roy Baumeister, found that negative events and remarks usually affect people more strongly than positive ones of similar size.
story:
The pottery shed at Camp Wren smelled like wet dog and minerals, and Ms. Traoré ran it like a small democracy where everyone got a vote on everyone else's work. Every Friday the wheel students put their pieces on the long pine table and the whole group offered feedback, which was the part Juliette dreaded more than the kiln, which had once cracked a bowl so loudly that a counselor came running from the lake.

Juliette was competent at clay. She could center a lump and pull a wall without collapsing it, and she knew what she was looking at when she looked at other people's pieces. That was the problem. Nora, who slept in the cot next to hers and had taught her to braid her hair with two strings, had spent all week on a tall vase with a rim that wandered to the left like a lost dog, and on Friday it would sit on that table, and Juliette would be asked what she thought.

"Just say it's nice," Linkin advised. He was in the woodshop group and had opinions about everything, most of them borrowed from his older brother. His father was on furlough from the plant in Melford, which was why Linkin was at Wren instead of the lake trip his brother kept describing, in tones of genuine reverence, as the most hedonistic week a sixteen-year-old could legally have. "Nora knows her rim's crooked. She doesn't need you to tell her."

"But it's not just crooked," Juliette said. "The proportions are good. The glaze test tiles she did are the best in the group. And the rim is fixable if she cuts it back to a clean line before it dries any further." She had started trying to parametrize the problem on paper, which she knew was ridiculous: she'd drawn a little chart with columns for what worked and what didn't, as though honesty were a machine you could set the dials on. The chart said nothing about Nora's face, which was the part that actually worried her.

She had a reason to worry, and it wasn't a vague one. Two summers ago, at swim club, a coach had watched her flip turn, told her five things she'd done well and one thing she did wrong, and Juliette had walked home remembering only the wrong thing. She had replayed it for weeks, the elbow dropping early, and the compliments had evaporated like rain on a hot sidewalk. She'd mentioned it once to her mother, who said people were strange, and that had been the end of it. But here in the camp library, killing an afternoon under a fan, she'd found a photocopied chapter in a battered binder, a review of research led by a man named Roy Baumeister, published in 2001, and the title at the top of the page had explained her whole flip turn: "Bad Is Stronger Than Good."

"That's the name of it," she told Linkin, dropping the binder on his bunk. "Some review, 2001. Baumeister and other researchers. They found that negative events and remarks usually affect people more strongly than positive ones of similar size." Linkin read the title, then read her chart, then looked at her with something close to pity. "Similar size," he said. "So if you tell her four nice things and one bad thing, she weighs the bad one like it's a piano."

"So I put the piano in a smaller room," Juliette said. "I say one thing, exactly, and I say it in a way she can use." Linkin pointed out that this was not how the finding worked, and Juliette pointed out that she wasn't running a study, she was trying to keep a friend and fix a rim, and that the two projects could overlap without being identical. She sat with that thought for a while, turning it over the way she turned clay, and decided she believed it about eighty percent, and that the remaining twenty percent she would have to find out the hard way.

Friday came. Nora's vase stood on the pine table with its wandering rim, and when it was her turn Juliette heard herself say, evenly, that the glaze test tiles were the best in the group and she wanted to know the recipe, and that the walls had an even thickness all the way up, which was harder than it looked. Then, before her nerve could reorganize itself: "The rim pulls left starting about a third of the way around. If you cut it back to a level line tonight, before it's fully dry, the whole silhouette squares up." She stopped there. No cushioning, no apology, no third compliment to bury the correction under.

Nora turned the vase slowly, found the leftward drift with her thumb, and nodded once. "A third of the way around," she said. "Yeah. I kept losing my anchor hand." She carried the vase to the workbench and came back with the fettling knife, and Ms. Traoré, who had watched the whole exchange without expression, picked up the little recipe card Nora had left beside the tiles and began, unhurriedly, to read it.

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
knowledge_domain: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
fact: A Marxist reading often asks whose labour makes the characters' comfortable lives possible, noticing servants and workers the novel mentions only in passing.
story:
The book club met in the back room of the library on Tuesday evenings, and Antoine arrived early with two novels, a legal pad, and the feeling that he was about to be found out. He had spent the weekend learning something he could not yet name properly, and the legal pad held the evidence. In the third chapter of the book they had all been assigned, he had counted the servants. They were named eleven times. They spoke twice.

"Is that the book?" Eleni asked, dropping her bag on the table and nodding at the legal pad. "Or is that your manifesto?"

"It's notes," Antoine said, and turned the pad face down before he could decide whether that was true.

Mr. Francis, who ran the club and taught English at the high school, had given them a single instruction for this meeting: come prepared to argue that the novel meant something other than what it appeared to mean. Marshall, who had known Antoine since sixth grade and enjoyed his discomfort more than most people's company, had predicted that Antoine would bring a summary of the plot and try to pass it off as an interpretation. Antoine had not spoken to him for a day after that, and then, privately, had decided that Marshall had a point, which was exactly why he had gone looking for something better.

The discussion started the way it always started, with Eleni defending the heroine's choices and Marshall poking at the plot's conveniences. Antoine waited, thumbing the corner of the legal pad, until Eleni said the ballroom scene showed the family at its happiest.

"There are four people carrying trays in that scene," Antoine said. "We're told their clothes. We're never told their names."

"They're background," Marshall said.

"That's the thing." Antoine turned the pad over and slid it to the middle of the table. "A Marxist reading asks whose labour makes the characters' comfortable lives possible. It notices the servants and workers the novel mentions only in passing. So I counted. In this chapter, the servants are named eleven times and they speak twice. Once to announce a visitor and once to say the carriage is ready."

Nobody said anything. Mr. Francis leaned back in his chair with the particular stillness Antoine had learned to distrust, the stillness of a teacher deciding whether to rescue a student or let him keep walking.

"So the whole elegant world of this book," Eleni said slowly, "is underpinned by people the book can't be bothered to hear from."

"Eleven mentions, two lines of speech," Antoine said. "You could argue the novel knows and doesn't care. Or you could argue the not-caring is the point. I can't decide which, and I read the chapter three times."

"You sound like you did actual work," Marshall said. "For a book club."

"It was subterfuge," Antoine admitted. "I thought if I had numbers, nobody could say I was just describing the plot again. The numbers were supposed to do the arguing for me. Then the numbers turned out to be interesting, and now I actually have to argue."

Mr. Francis cleared his throat. "For what it's worth, the assumption that interpretation is a matter of taste is not axiomatic. Some readings account for more of the text than others. Mr. Antoine's reading accounts for two lines of speech that the rest of us skipped."

"Two lines," Eleni said. She pulled her own copy toward her and began flipping pages, and for a while the meeting turned into something Antoine had never seen it become: three people bent over one chapter, hunting for every waiter and carriage driver and girl with a lamp, arguing about whether a figure in a doorway counted as a servant or a guest's attendant, Marshall insisting that half the mentions were duplicates until Antoine made him recount them aloud.

The meeting ran fifteen minutes long. When the librarian knocked on the door frame to close up, Eleni was copying the page numbers of the servant scenes into her phone, and Marshall was holding the legal pad up to the light as if it might contain a second layer.

"You're taking that home?" Antoine asked.

"Photocopying it," Marshall said. "Some of us have chem homework and no time to read chapters three times."

Antoine gathered his books, pleased in a way he could not fully separate from vanity, and it was only in the parking lot, when Eleni caught up to him, that the evening's arithmetic turned on him.

"One question," she said. "Who typed up your notes this weekend?"

"My mom. Why?"

"Your mom typed them." Eleni zipped her bag. "So the essay about invisible labour that made everybody actually think for once, exists because your mother spent her Sunday at your desk while you read."

Antoine stood holding both novels against his chest, the legal pad gone, the cold coming through his jacket.

"I'm going to count that," he said.

"Eleven," Eleni said, and walked toward her car.

activity: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
knowledge_domain: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
fact: Doubling the size of a sorted list adds only one extra step to a binary search, while it doubles the worst-case work of a linear search.
story:
The basement smelled like solder and the ghost of last summer's flood, and Andrew had been staring at the same line of code for eleven minutes when Trystan finally leaned over his shoulder and said, "You know it's not going to apologize to you, right?"

"I'm not waiting for an apology. I'm waiting for it to make sense." Andrew turned the laptop so Trystan could see the function he'd written that afternoon, a plain loop that walked down the team's parts list one row at a time, hunting for a single part number. It worked. It had always worked. That was the problem, or at least it was the problem once Megane came clattering down the stairs with her phone held out like a verdict.

"Inventory came in," she said. "Guess how many line items now."

"Three hundred?"

"Six hundred and four. The other team merged their spreadsheet into ours because Ms. Fitzgerald said sharing is a virtue." Megane dropped onto the couch beside a half-disassembled claw mechanism. "So your lookup thing still fast, or are we doing the thing where the robot stands there like a boreal owl in January, perfectly silent, perfectly useless?"

Trystan laughed, and Andrew, despite himself, laughed too, because the robot really did do that: when the lookup dragged, the whole arm hung mid-air, patient and blank, waiting for an answer that arrived too late to matter. He ran the search on the old list, then on the new one, and the timer told a story he didn't enjoy. On three hundred rows it had taken a comfortable handful of milliseconds. On six hundred and four, it took roughly twice as long. He ran it again to be sure. Twice as long, again, like a bill arriving in duplicate.

"That's the worst part," Megane said, not unkindly. "The list got twice as big overnight, and your thing got twice as slow. That's not a coincidence, is it. That's just arithmetic being rude."

Andrew was quiet for a moment, not because he was hurt but because something was assembling itself at the back of his mind. He'd been reading, late at night, the way he read when a problem mesmerized him and the tabs multiplied like pond life. Somewhere in one of those tabs there had been a different way to find a thing in a sorted list, and the word "sorted" was suddenly loud, because he'd spent two hours last week sorting the parts list by part number and had then forgotten he'd done it, the way you forget infrastructure. "The list is sorted," he said. "We sorted it. I sorted it. It's sorted."

"Congratulations," said Trystan. "Was that a status update or a plan?"

"A plan." Andrew pulled up a blank editor window and started typing, and the other two watched the way people watch someone juggle, with fondness and a readiness to duck. He would look at the middle of the list first, he was saying aloud, half to them and half to the code. If the part number he wanted came before the middle, he could throw away the entire back half. If it came after, he could throw away the front. Either way, half the list vanished in a single comparison. Then he did it again, on whatever remained. He was describing it with his hands now, chopping the air into smaller and smaller pieces, and Megane said, "You look like you're conducting a very small, very angry orchestra," and he said, "Shh, the violins are halving."

He got it wrong twice before he got it right. The first version had an off-by-one error that sent the search circling the same three rows forever, and Trystan diagnosed it by leaning in and saying, with theatrical sorrow, "It's staring at the same shelf. It loves that shelf. It will never leave that shelf." The second version crashed outright on an empty range, and Andrew fixed that one himself, hunched close, muttering. The third version ran, and they loaded the old list of three hundred, and the timer reported a number so small Megane made him run it five more times because she didn't believe it once.

Then the real test. Six hundred and four rows, the doubled list, the one that had punished his old function so precisely. He ran the new search on it and sat back, and for a second nobody said anything, because the number on the screen was almost exactly what it had been for three hundred rows. One comparison more, give or take, where the old way had paid double. "Wait," Megane said, pulling the laptop toward herself as if the timer might be lying to her personally. "The list doubled and it did one extra step. One." She looked up. "That's not supposed to be allowed."

"That's the whole trade," Andrew said, and even he could hear that he'd crossed from annoyed into evangelical. "The old way reads every row in the worst case, so double the rows, double the reading. This one cuts the list in half every step, so doubling the size of a sorted list just adds one more step. One." He tapped the screen on the two timers, old list and new, sitting there nearly identical. Trystan said, "So the lesson is I should have let you sort things months ago," and Andrew said, "The lesson is the sorting was the lesson," and Megane groaned and threw a cushion at both of them.

They spent another hour wiring the new lookup into the robot's control code, and Megane kept a running commentary on the pragmatics of their situation, how it was all very well to be fast in theory but the arm still needed to not crush the practice cubes, which was a separate virtue entirely. Somewhere upstairs a door opened and closed. At ten past midnight, the basement lights flickered the way they always did when the furnace woke up, and Trystan's phone buzzed with a text from Ms. Fitzgerald, who apparently never slept: Did the inventory merge break anything?

Andrew looked at the two functions side by side on the screen, the slow one and the fast one, both still there in the file because he hadn't deleted the old version yet. "Tell her it broke the slow one," he said. "Tell her the fast one didn't notice."

Megane typed the reply, then held the phone up so they could all see what she'd written: The robot noticed nothing. It is an owl. It is serene. Then she set the phone face-down on the claw mechanism, and the three of them watched the little status light on the robot's board blink, steady and unhurried, like it had all the time in the world.

activity: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
knowledge_domain: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
fact: Deuteronomy 22:8 commands building a parapet around a flat roof so that no one falls, and Jewish tradition extends the rule to other hazards on one's property.
story:
The thing I remembered best about my grandfather's shul was the roof, which was flat and edged with a low railing, and I had never once thought about why until Ms. Berg assigned us our debate topics on Tuesday night. That was the version I told Wyatt later, anyway, that the memory arrived whole and obvious, though honestly the roof came back to me in pieces, over hours, while I sat in the social hall copying verses onto index cards. What I transcribed first was Deuteronomy 22:8, because Ms. Berg had circled it on my topic sheet with a note that said only: build your argument from the text. When you build a new house, the verse says, make a parapet around your roof, so that you may not bring the guilt of bloodshed on your house if anyone should fall from it. I read it four times. I had been assigned to argue that this rule, written for flat roofs in a world of mud brick and goats, still applied now, and I had volunteered for that side only because Grant had rolled his eyes when it came up and I wanted to wipe the roll off his face.

Wyatt found me at the folding table with the index cards fanned out like a losing poker hand. "You know the roof rule is why my dad had to put a fence around our pool," he said. He dropped into the chair across from me and stole my pen. "Not the roof part. The whole principle. My rabbi called it a fence around danger. It's not just roofs in the tradition. It's anything on your property that could hurt somebody." I told him that sounded grandiose for a pool fence, and he said maybe, but his little cousin had still not drowned in it, so. He said it lightly, the way he said most things, and I laughed, and then I remembered that I was supposed to be building a case, not making friends with the other side, because Wyatt had drawn the opposing argument: that a three-thousand-year-old verse about parapets cannot meaningfully govern a world of zoning codes and liability insurance. He knew it was a strong position. He told me so twice, generously, which was worse than taunting me.

Here is what I did not tell anyone that week: I already knew the roof rule. Not from Ms. Berg's packet. From the summer I was nine, when my father stood on the flat roof of our building replacing a vent cap and my mother stood below him on the sidewalk repeating a sentence in Hebrew, over and over, like a spell, until he came down. I asked her once what it meant and she said it was about railings, about not letting people fall, and I thought she was making it up to scare him into being careful. I thought that for years. So when Ms. Berg handed me the verse I pretended it was new to me, and I pretended, even to myself, that the flutter I felt was competitive nerves. I was almost thirty percent sure it was competitive nerves.

Wyatt, meanwhile, had gone home and done the reading, and by Thursday he had a problem. He showed up at the social hall with his laptop and a face like a man delivering bad news about a beloved dog. "My whole case was going to be that it's obsolete," he said. "Rooftops aren't living space anymore, nobody's hosting dinner up there, the hazard the verse names basically doesn't exist." He turned the laptop toward Alexa. "Except the tradition doesn't stay on the roof. It keeps extending. Stairs, ladders, my dad's pool. I can't argue it's obsolete when the rule keeps proving it isn't." He said this with genuine anguish, and she understood that he wanted her to release him from it, and she also understood that if she did, she would win on Thursday without having won anything.

"Then argue the other thing," Alexa said slowly, and watched his face change. "Not that the rule is dead. That it's too small. Insurance and building codes already do this better than the verse does. The tradition extends it, fine, but the state already extended it further." She had not planned to hand him this. The words had come out on their own, assembled out of everything she'd been reading, and there was a bitter satisfaction in it, the kind you get from being right against your own side.

The debate itself was held in the sanctuary after services, which felt like arguing in front of a very patient grandparent. Grant, who was not in the class but came for the food afterward, sat in the second row. Ms. Berg sat in the back with her grading folder closed on her lap, which Alexa chose to read as trust. Wyatt went first and was better than she expected: he argued that a rule carried forward by tradition is a rule already admitting its letter is insufficient, so the letter cannot be the authority. Then Alexa stood up, and her notes were in her hand, and she found she did not look at them.

She talked about her grandfather's shul, the flat roof with its railing, because that was the safest memory available and she was not going to stand in a sanctuary and tell twenty people about her father on the vent cap. She said the verse does something building codes don't: it attaches the guilt to the owner, to the person, before any accident happens. A code tells you what to build. The verse tells you who you become if you don't. She said the tradition extending the rule to other hazards on one's property was not the rule shrinking to fit modern life but modern life being read through the rule, which was a different direction of travel than anyone had argued yet. Then she stopped, because the next sentence in her head was about her mother on the sidewalk, and she let the silence sit for a second before sitting down.

Ms. Berg did not declare a winner. She asked them each one question, wrote something, and said the class would vote next week, a plebiscite Alexa found almost comically solemn for a room of twelve teenagers, and then everyone went to the folding table for rugelach. Grant told her she'd won, definitively, and Wyatt said Grant would say that about anyone who beat him at anything, and the three of them stood by the window while the sky went down over the parking lot.

She never told Wyatt about the roof of her building. She told herself this was strategy, or privacy, or that the moment had simply never come, and she believed it about three quarters of the way, which for Alexa was a fairly high percentage. On the walk home she passed the construction site at Fourth and Mineral, where a new apartment building was going up, flat-roofed, the parapet forms already in place, plywood and rebar outlined against the last light. She stood at the fence a while. Then she texted Wyatt a single question mark, deleted it, and kept walking, and behind her the cranes stood very still over the unfinished edge.

activity: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
knowledge_domain: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
