fact: In a major-key movement in sonata form, the exposition's second theme is usually in the dominant key, so a movement in C major moves to G major.
story:
Kaylee spread the score of Mozart's Piano Sonata in C major across the music desk in Ms. Wanjiru's studio, weighting the curling pages with a mug of pencils and a rubber eraser shaped like a frog. On the page were three pencil marks she had made herself: exposition, development, recapitulation, each word written in the margin with more confidence than she felt. Ms. Wanjiru had said only, "Play it and tell me where you think the boundaries are," and then gone to the window to water a geranium that had been dead since October.

She played the opening, the little broken chords she had learned at nine, and came to the place where a new tune arrived, brighter and busier than the first. Her pencil hovered. She had marked that spot as the start of the second theme, but she could not have said why, except that it sounded like a second theme. Ms. Wanjiru, still holding the watering can over the dead geranium, said, "Check the key signature there. What has it moved to?"

Kaylee bent over the score. The tune sat one line lower than the opening had, on different notes, with a sharp appearing where before there had been none. "G major," she said. "It's gone to G major." She remembered the rule as it settled into place, the kind of fact that sits in you like sedimentary rock, laid down in layers by old teachers and only visible when something cuts through it. "The second theme usually goes to the dominant. So in C major, that's G."

"Usually," Ms. Wanjiru said, and set the can down.

Harnoor, who had her lesson after Kaylee's and had let herself in ten minutes ago, was sprawled on the studio's one armchair with her trumpet case across her knees. "You know what I like about Mozart?" she said. "He got paid. Composers now, my cousin does it, he scores indie games for exposure. Exposure is how you die of cold." Harnoor wanted to switch her audition piece from the Haydn concerto to something modern, and had been lobbying Ms. Wanjiru for two weeks, and had brought, as evidence, a recording on her phone that she kept almost playing and then not playing, saving it, Kaylee suspected, for the moment of maximum effect.

"Usually means there are exceptions," Ms. Wanjiru said. She came to the piano and turned back several pages. "So if the new tune arrives and it is still in C, what then?"

"Then it's not a second theme yet," Kaylee said slowly. "It's, like, a transition pretending." She looked again at her mark. The passage she had labelled as the second theme's beginning actually had two stages: first the C major material twisting and pushing, then the new tune arriving properly, settled into G, at home there. She erased her mark and drew it four bars later. The eraser frog rolled off the desk and Harnoor caught it without looking up from her phone.

"Here's the thing though," Kaylee said, and stopped, because she was not sure the thing was a thing. Ms. Wanjiru waited the way she waited, arms folded, letting silence do the work. "When I just listen, I don't hear a key change. I hear a new tune. But when I look, the key change is what proves it's a new theme. So which one is the actual fact, the sound or the page?" She knew enough to know this was an old argument wearing new clothes, the ear against the logos of the score, and she knew enough to know she was not going to settle it before 4:30.

Harnoor held up her phone. "Play this for her," she said to Ms. Wanjiru. "Forty seconds. It's a piece written last year for trumpet and piano, there's a key change in it that made me cry on a bus." Ms. Wanjiru took the phone, looked at the timer, and said, "Two minutes, because Kaylee still owes me a recapitulation."

Kaylee turned to the final section. The opening tune came back in C major, right where she had marked it, and she played it through with her pencil resting on the exact bar. Then she noticed something else, a small passage in the middle of the recapitulation that did not appear in the exposition at all, and she wrote a question mark beside it in handwriting much smaller than her other marks. "This part's new," she said. "Or I missed it the first time. I'm not sure which."

Ms. Wanjiru put Harnoor's phone on the piano lid, speaker up. "Then leave the question mark," she said. "It's the most honest thing on the page." She pressed play.

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: JUnit's assertEquals takes the expected value first and the actual value second, so swapping them gives confusing failure messages.
story:
The library had a back corner where the computers were older than the ones at school, and Mathis had claimed one for three Saturdays running. He was building a class called Song with three private fields, title, artist, and lengthInSeconds, and he had promised Francis he would show it off by Monday, because Francis had already finished his own version and would not stop mentioning it. The promise was the easy part. The class itself was coming along: private fields, a constructor, getter methods named getTitle and getArtist and getLengthInSeconds, each returning its value like a courier handing over a sealed envelope. What Mathis could not get working was the test.

He had written a JUnit test in the library's blue-lit quiet, an assertEquals line for every getter, and when he ran it, two of the three passed. The third failed with a message he read six times before it began to feel personal. The test said it expected 213 but got 212. Mathis knew the song. He had timed it himself, twice, and the length was 212 seconds. He had typed 212 into the test with his own hands. So where, he wanted to ask the screen, had 213 come from. He sat very still, the way his geology teacher said you should when you found something odd in a rock face, because the strange thing was usually the doorway to the interesting thing, the way a vein of igneous rock cutting through older stone meant something had forced its way up from below.

Aaliyah dropped into the chair beside him with her bag still on her shoulder. "Francis says you're stuck."

"Francis says a lot." He turned the screen toward her. "Read that failure message. Tell me what you see."

She leaned in, chewed the end of her pen, read it aloud. "Expected 213, actual 212." She glanced at him. "So?"

"So I never wrote 213. Anywhere. Not in the class, not in the test. It's like the number came from nowhere."

"It has provenance," Aaliyah said, which was a word she'd picked up from a documentary about stolen paintings and used for anything whose origin mattered. "Numbers don't just appear. You typed it, or the computer thinks you did."

That was the thought that had been circling him for half an hour, refusing to land. He opened the test file again and read the line character by character, the way Ms. Pham, who ran the Saturday coding drop-in at the table by the windows, had told them to do when a failure made no sense. Read it like a stranger, she'd said. Not like the person who wrote it, because the person who wrote it will read what they meant instead of what's there. The line looked correct. It looked correct in the way a face in a photograph looks like the person you know, until you notice the eyes are wrong.

He closed his eyes for a second and recited the line from memory. assertEquals, then two hundred and thirteen, comma, song dot getLengthInSeconds. He opened his eyes and read the line on the screen. The order was reversed. In his memory he had always put the class first and the number second, natural as putting a letter before its envelope, but the actual line had the number first and the method call second. And the failure message, the thing that had baffled him, suddenly had a shape: it printed the first argument as the expected value and the second as the actual value, so with his arguments swapped, the message called the expected thing what was really the result of the getter, and the actual thing what was really the number he'd chosen. That was the whole mystery. Not a ghost in the machine. An order of arguments.

Aaliyah was watching his face. "You look like you found the vein."

"The order," he said. "Expected first, actual second. I put them backwards, so the failure message calls 212 the actual value when 212 is really my expected, and it calls what my getter returned the expected, which is backwards too." He said it fast and then slowed, testing it against the message one more time, and it held. Still, a small uneasiness stayed with him, and he was honest enough with himself to notice it: he did not know why the library's tutorial had put the number first, and he could not remember which convention Francis used, and tomorrow he might mix them up again, because understanding a trap once did not mean you never stepped in it twice. What he had was a considered position built from two ideas stitched together, his own stubborn certainty that the class was right, and Aaliyah's insistence that the number had to come from somewhere. Neither idea alone had found it.

He swapped the arguments, saved, and ran the tests. Three green bars. He sat back and let out a breath he hadn't known he was holding, and Aaliyah put out her fist and he bumped it.

"Show Francis," she said. "Make him sweat first. Tell him it was a bug in the compiler."

Mathis laughed, then pulled the keyboard toward himself again. "No. I'll show him the line." He began writing a fourth test, this time for a null title, typing the arguments slowly, number first, method call second, reading each character like a stranger.

activity: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
knowledge_domain: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
fact: The area between two curves is found by integrating the upper function minus the lower function over the interval where they are ordered that way.
story:
The library smelled of warm dust and the glue of old bindings, and Keira had claimed the table by the window where the afternoon light fell flat across the graph paper. She was there because Ms. Torres had left a note in her mailbox: Math club, Thursday, the integration unit, you'll want this before September. Keira had not decided yet whether she wanted it. Calculus had been the one class where her mind went white with static, and she had signed up for it anyway in the fall, out of a stubbornness she could not entirely explain, not even to Janna, who had asked her twice why she would do that to herself.

Janna arrived first, Francis a minute behind her with a laminated sheet of problems the club kept in a drawer nobody was supposed to open without permission, which Francis had opened without permission. "Two curves," he said, laying the sheet between them. "A line and a parabola. They want the area trapped between them." He slid his notebook over. "I got four thirds."

Janna frowned at her own page. "I got negative four thirds." She turned the notebook so the others could see the long chain of antiderivatives, the careful limits, the arithmetic that had consumed most of her free period. "Same interval. Same functions. I checked the arithmetic twice."

"Then one of you imputed the fault to the wrong place," Keira said, and immediately regretted the phrasing, which had come out of her mother's vocabulary, not her own. What she meant was simpler: everyone kept hunting for a dropped sign or a botched multiplication, and her instinct said the error lived somewhere earlier, somewhere more structural. She pulled the sheet toward her and copied both curves onto fresh paper, the parabola opening upward, the line cutting across it so that together they fenced in a single closed pocket.

She had spent the summer on the disbursement of her scholarship, checking the portal every morning to see whether the money had moved from the college's account to hers, and she understood in a vague, inchoate way that the university wanted her to arrive already knowing this material. Ms. Torres, shelving returns two aisles over, had said as much without saying it: she had simply left the note. So Keira sat with the two graphs and did not touch the algebra at all. She shaded the pocket between the curves with the side of her pencil, lightly, until the whole trapped region was gray.

"Look," she said. "Inside the pocket, the line is above the parabola. The whole way across. It doesn't cross back."

"So?" Francis said, but he was already leaning in.

"So the area has to come out positive, no matter what. It's an area." She tapped Janna's page, then Francis's. "You subtracted in different orders. Janna took the parabola minus the line, and Francis took the line minus the parabola, and the line is on top the whole way, so the top one minus the bottom one is the one that comes out right." She said it slowly, testing the sentence as she went, and found that she believed it. "Whoever put the upper function on the bottom got the negative."

Janna flipped back a page and ran her finger down her work. "I did. Parabola minus line. Francis had the line first." She looked up. "Negative four thirds and four thirds. Same magnitude. It was the order the entire time."

"Which means I was right," Francis said.

"Which means you were lucky," Janna said, but she was laughing, and Keira noticed that neither of them had gone back to hunting for arithmetic errors, which was its own small vindication. Keira recopied the integral with the line first and the parabola second, evaluated it at both limits, and got four thirds, and then, because trust in a method built only once was no trust at all, she re-derived it from the beginning and got four thirds again. The answer held.

Ms. Torres came past with a cart of biography, paused, and looked at the shaded pocket on Keira's page. She said nothing about the math. She said, "The window table gets cold around four, there's a vent under it," and rolled the cart on toward the 900s.

Keira sat with the finished page a while. It was not lost on her that a thing could be true and still feel provisional, that she could hold the rule firmly, upper minus lower where the upper was genuinely the upper, and at the same time not know whether she could find it again alone, at night, in a lecture hall of three hundred. That part stayed uncertain, and she let it stay. She tore the page carefully along the perforation, folded it once, and put it in the front pocket of her notebook where the scholarship letter lived.

"Same time next Thursday," Janna said, closing her binder. "There's a sheet with three curves on it. Overlapping ones."

"Then we'll find out which one is on top where," Keira said, and she squared the stack of graph paper against the table's edge.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: The US federal minimum wage has been $7.25 an hour since July 24, 2009, though many states and cities set a higher minimum.
story:
The application had asked for his shirt size, which Samuel found stranger than anything else on the form. He sat in a booth at the diner with the pen they had given him, a pen chained to a clipboard, and wrote his name in letters smaller than usual, as though the whole arrangement might still be reversible. Behind the counter, a man in a paper hat slid two eggs onto a plate without looking at them. Samuel had eaten here maybe thirty times in his life, always from the other side of the counter, and it had never once occurred to him that the place ran on people his age carrying plates of eggs.

"You're hired if you can start Saturday," the man said, reading the form upside down. "Busser. Seven twenty-five an hour."

Samuel said okay before he had finished deciding. On the walk home he practiced saying the number out loud, and it sounded smaller each time, the way a word repeated too often starts coming apart.

Treyton had gotten a job the same week, at a burger place one town over, one state line over, though the border was nothing but a river you could miss if you blinked on the bridge. Saturday night they sat on the hood of Treyton's brother's car in the diner lot, and Treyton unfolded his first paycheck like it was something he had smuggled out. "Nine forty an hour," he said. "Look." Samuel held his own check next to it and did the subtraction in his head. Same work, same month, two dollars and fifteen cents apart, and the distance between them was a bridge maybe a quarter mile long.

"That can't be legal," Treyton said. "Same job. It has to be the same."

They argued about it for a while, the way they argued about everything, and Samuel kept circling back to something his geometry teacher, Ms. Horváth, had said in the spring, that the small thing you prove on the way to the big thing is called a lemma, and that you couldn't skip it just because it looked minor. He didn't say the word out loud. But he was thinking that the paycheck was the minor thing, and something bigger waited behind it, and he couldn't get to the bigger thing without settling this one first.

He settled it in the break room on Monday, on his phone, while the dish machine rattled through its cycle. The federal minimum wage was $7.25 an hour, and it had been $7.25 since July 24, 2009, which was before either of them was born. But states and cities could set a higher minimum, and Treyton's state had, and Samuel's had not, and so the same hour of the same work was worth two different numbers depending on which side of the river you stood on. He read it twice. It was legal. It was simply legal, in the flat way that certain facts are legal, and he understood at once why his mother had been reticent about the whole subject when he'd told her his rate. She hadn't said it was unfair. She had said, "That's what they pay here," and changed the subject to his schedule.

At the same time, and he tried to hold both thoughts at once the way you hold two grocery bags, the job was his. Nobody had subjugated him into taking it; he had walked in, filled out the chained-up form, and said okay. When Elaina came in Tuesday after her rehearsal and sat in his section, because it was his section now, and ordered the pancakes she always ordered, he felt something complicated and undignified, which was pride. He brought her extra syrup without being asked. She left a dollar-fifty on the table and he cleared it and did not tell Treyton about it, and did not examine why.

He did tell Treyton the fact itself, on the bridge, because it was a Saturday and they had nowhere particular to be. "Seven twenty-five is the federal number," he said. "Since 2009. States and cities can go higher, and yours did." Treyton stood at the railing with his hands in his pockets and looked down at the water, which was the border and also just water.

"So crossing this bridge is worth two-fifteen an hour," Treyton said.

"I guess," Samuel said, and then, because it wasn't quite true, "I don't know if that's how to think about it. The job's still the job on either side."

Treyton flicked a pebble off the railing and they both watched it go. Somewhere behind them a car crossed the state line without slowing down, and neither of them turned around.

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: Research by linguist Paul Nation and colleagues suggests readers need to know about 98 percent of the words in a text to understand it comfortably without help.
story:
The laminated menu at Kis Bögre had photographs, which Zoe appreciated, because the photographs let her pretend she could read. She had chosen the restaurant for its name alone, back in September, when she signed up for the evening Hungarian class at the community centre and decided she needed somewhere to practise between Tuesdays. Mr. Horváth, who taught the class and also owned the restaurant, had laughed at that. "You will order the same goulash until you hate it," he said, "and then you will order it again, because it is the only word you know." She had proved him right for four months.

On Sunday her grandmother was coming to dinner, and her grandmother had one subject: the flood in her village, which Zoe had only ever heard about in English, in her grandmother's translated, embittered versions. Zoe wanted to read the actual coverage, the Hungarian coverage, and then summarise it aloud on Sunday, in Hungarian, the way Mr. Horváth had been drilling them all term. Read, close the paper, say it back in your own words. He called the exercise the bridge between decoding and owning the language, though mostly it felt like being asked to juggle while drowning.

She spread the newspaper across the table by the window, where Thierry was wiping down the counter. Thierry had taken the class with her for two weeks in October before quitting to take a shift here, and he still remembered enough to be dangerous. He leaned over her shoulder, squinted at the front page, and winced on her behalf.

"That's the one you picked? The lead story?" He tapped the headline. "That's not reading, that's archaeology." He dropped into the booth across from her without asking, still holding his rag. "You know what Mr. Horváth told me before I dropped out? There's this research, by a linguist named Paul Nation and some colleagues, and it says you need to know about ninety-eight percent of the words in a text to understand it comfortably without help. Ninety-eight. That leaves you, what, two unknown words per hundred, and you can limp through." He pointed at the article. "Count your unknowns in one paragraph of that."

She counted. The first paragraph was eight lines long and she could identify, generously, eleven words, one of which was "and," one of which was "the." "So that's not ten percent," she said. "That's maybe fifteen."

"That's a puzzle, not an article. You're not reading it. Nobody could." He said it without cruelty, the way you'd tell someone their shoe was untied, and then he got up because a table of four had come in near the door, and she was alone with the turbid grey typeface and her stack of flashcards.

She tried anyway, because she was stubborn and because Sunday was coming. She looked up word after word on her phone, built the first sentence painstakingly, and then reached the second sentence and found that the first had already gone soft in her memory, like wet sand. This was the part nobody warned you about, the part that all the motivational posters about practice had bromided past: that effort alone, applied to a text beyond you, produced nothing but fatigue. She pushed the paper away and put her forehead on the table, briefly, and felt the cool of the Formica against her skin.

Then she turned to page six, which she had skipped because the story there was small and, she'd assumed, unimportant: three short paragraphs about the same flood, from the regional paper, written in simple declaratives. She read the first sentence and understood it. Not every word; there was a verb she didn't know and a noun she half-knew, but the sentence held together, carried her to its period, and stayed put in her mind afterward. She read the paragraph again, closed her eyes, and said it back to the empty booth in her clanking accent: the river reached the church, the water stood two days, the people returned Thursday. It was crude. It was also, unmistakably, a summary, hers, and the feeling that followed was one she could only call exhilarating, as if she had been holding her breath for four months and had finally exhaled.

She did the second paragraph, then the third, slower, losing the thread once and finding it. When Thierry came back with a plate he swore he had not ordered for her but which clearly contained goulash, she summarised the whole article for him, haltingly, watching his face to see whether the words were landing. He listened all the way through, which was more courtesy than the words probably deserved, and then he said, "The church part I got. The Thursday, maybe. Say the river sentence again."

She said it again, and this time it came out in one breath, whole. Behind her, a voice said something in Hungarian, fast and warm and amused, and she turned to find the waitress standing there with a coffee pot, grinning at her, waiting as though Zoe had been addressed and an answer was expected.

"Ezt én írtam," the waitress said, and pointed at page six, at the three paragraphs, and then at herself. Then, in English, delighted: "The reporter. My second job."

activity: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
knowledge_domain: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
fact: Near the end of the development, a retransition often dwells on the home key's dominant chord, building an expectation that the tonic and the first theme are about to return.
story:
Juliette had been acclimating to Ms. Pelletier's studio for three weeks now, which mostly meant learning not to flinch when the metronome on the piano leapt to life on its own, some ancient electric tremor nobody had ever bothered to fix. The room smelled of rosin and instant coffee. The clock ran ten minutes fast, on purpose, Ms. Pelletier claimed, "to keep us honest." On the table between them lay a photocopied score of a Mozart piano sonata movement, its margins blank and accusing, and beside it Juliette's pencil, sharpened to a point that suggested violence.

"For Saturday," Ms. Pelletier had said at the last lesson, "you will tell me where the exposition ends, where the development begins, and where the recapitulation shows up. If you get it wrong, nothing terrible happens. If you guess, something terrible happens." She had not defined terrible. Juliette had not asked.

Noah was there because his lesson was after hers and because he never arrived anywhere on time except when it let him loiter. He lay along the piano bench like a discarded coat, scrolling his phone. "You're going to fail," he said pleasantly.

"I'm going to receive an acquittal," Juliette said. "Full marks. Acquitted of all charges of musical illiteracy."

"That's not what acquittal means for a test."

"It's what it means for me."

Ms. Pelletier dropped the needle on the turntable in the corner, an actual turntable, and the movement began. Juliette listened the way she had trained herself to over three Saturdays: following the first theme like a dog on a leash, watching the second theme arrive in a new key, feeling the exposition close its doors. She made her first mark. "There," she said. "Exposition ends, development starts."

The development did what developments do, which was to take every familiar scrap of tune and behave badly with it. It turned pugnacious, fists up, knocking the themes around through keys they had never agreed to visit. Noah sat up slightly, which for Noah was roughly a standing ovation. Juliette's pencil hovered, waiting for the moment that mattered, the one Ms. Pelletier kept circling without naming.

Then she heard it. The music slowed and settled onto one chord and simply stayed there, circling, insisting, the harmony leaning forward in its chair, and Juliette found herself leaning forward too, because it sounded exactly as if the opening tune, the first theme, everything, was about to walk back through the door. Her whole body was certain of it. She scribbled a mark and wrote, fast, before the certainty could be contradicted: "dominant chord, home key, near the end of the development." Under it, in smaller letters: "retransition." Then the music did what she'd been promised without being told: it delivered the tonic, and the first theme returned, and she sat back feeling insufferably pleased.

"That's the retransition," she said, pointing at her pencil mark when the side ended. "Near the end of the development. It just sits on the dominant and makes you wait."

Ms. Pelletier looked at the page for a long moment. She looked at the turntable. Then she did something Juliette had never seen her do, which was to laugh, briefly, into her closed hand. "Juliette," she said, "side two of that record is not Mozart."

The room went quiet in a way that made the metronome's tick suddenly very loud. Noah, on the bench, had developed an intense interest in the ceiling.

"Side two," Ms. Pelletier went on, "is a demo tape a student gave me years ago. A student who wrote a sonata movement for his college application. Who knew his forms cold, even then." She turned toward the bench. "Who apparently also knows how to press the record button on my turntable."

"You recorded over the Mozart?" Juliette said.

"I recorded over side two," Noah said, sitting up with great dignity, "which, for the record, was already scratched. And you marked the retransition correctly. On my piece. Which I wrote when I was seventeen." He pointed at her score, at her pencil note, at the dominant chord she had circled. "That's my chord. You heard it. You heard exactly what I built it for."

Juliette looked down at her own handwriting, at the smug little word retransition, at the whole argument of the page, and felt something between vindication and vertigo. She had been honest with the music and the music had been a forgery, except that it wasn't, not really, because it had done everything true.

"So," she said slowly, "did I pass?"

"That depends," said Ms. Pelletier. She flipped the record over, set the needle down, and folded her hands. "Side one. Real Mozart. Do it again."

Juliette picked up her pencil and leaned in as the first theme began.

activity: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
knowledge_domain: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
fact: In June 2013, documents leaked by Edward Snowden revealed that the US National Security Agency was collecting phone records, such as numbers called and call durations, of millions of Verizon customers.
story:
The group chat lit up at 11:14 p.m., which was late even for them. Naomi was lying on her bedroom floor with her history textbook open to a page she had read four times without absorbing, and the phone buzzed against her ribs like a second heartbeat. Gregory had posted a screenshot of a homework prompt: "Was Snowden a patriot or a traitor? Defend your position in 500 words." Beneath it he typed, "Mr. Nasser actually assigned this. Man is a virtuoso of ruining my week."

Kali's reply came in a burst of three messages. "idk. he leaked stuff so ppl would know what the government was doing. seems patriotic to me." Then, "also this is from like 2013 why do we care." Then a shrugging emoji. Naomi sat up. She knew almost nothing about it, which bothered her more than the assignment itself, because she could feel the debate forming already in the chat, Gregory already typing, and she did not want to be the one who only reacted.

She typed, "wait, what did he actually leak? like specifically." Kali answered with a link and a line she had copied from somewhere: "In June 2013, documents leaked by Edward Snowden revealed that the US National Security Agency was collecting phone records, such as numbers called and call durations, of millions of Verizon customers." Naomi read it twice. Numbers called. Call durations. She had expected something about missiles or undercover agents, something cinematic, and instead it was this: metadata, the boring skeleton of every ordinary conversation.

Gregory's message arrived before she could finish the thought. "so what. i have nothing to hide lol." It was such a comfortable sentence, and Naomi understood its comfort, the way it let you close the tab and go to sleep. But Kali replied, "ok but would you mind if i made a list of everyone you call? and how long you talk to them?" The chat went quiet for a full minute, the typing indicator appearing and disappearing as Gregory started and abandoned answers. Naomi watched the little dots pulse and die, pulse and die, and thought about what her own call log would say about her: who she called at two in the morning last spring, and how long those calls lasted, and what a stranger could infer from the pattern even without hearing a single word.

"I wouldn't like it," she finally typed, "but that's different from whether it's wrong." Gregory answered fast, relieved to have a foothold again. "it's national security. there's tradeoffs." Kali shot back, "you're prevaricating. you just said it doesn't matter and now it's a tradeoff. pick one." Naomi laughed out loud, alone in her room, and then stopped laughing, because Kali had a point and also didn't. Gregory wasn't lying exactly; he was doing what people do when a comfortable position starts to shift under them, and Naomi recognized it because she was doing it too.

She got up and opened her laptop. It took her twenty minutes of reading, past the hot takes and the defensive statements, to understand the shape of it: the phone records of millions of customers, collected wholesale, not because any of them was suspected of anything. She found a quote from the President's own review group saying the program had not been essential to preventing attacks, and she found defenders arguing that bulk collection was a tool you would regret losing. Both sides had evidence. Both sides were certain. She sat with that for a while, the ceiling fan turning above her, and typed slowly: "i think the problem isn't that someone reads my call log. it's that they could, all of it, forever, and i'd never know what got inferred from it. the list of everyone you call is a picture of you even if the calls are boring." Then, after a pause: "but i also think it's possible it kept some people safe. i don't know how to weigh that. i'm not going to pretend i do."

The chat held still. Then Gregory: "that's the most words you've ever typed in here." Then, separately, a minute later, more quietly for him: "my dad works at a hospital and their system flags patients it thinks won't show up for appointments. it's usually right. it's also usually right about the wrong reasons, like where they live. same thing kinda?" Naomi stared at that. It wasn't the same thing, exactly, but it wasn't different either, and the connection he had drawn was one she would not have made. She was still deciding what she thought about it when the phone buzzed again.

Mr. Nasser had posted to the whole class forum, apparently awake at midnight like the rest of them: "A hint for tomorrow. The best essays will not choose patriot or traitor. They will ask what we gave up, who decided, and whether we would have agreed if anyone had asked us." Kali sent, "he's watching this chat isn't he," and Gregory sent, "it's a group chat not a surveillance program," and then, a beat later, "probably."

Naomi smiled and closed the laptop halfway, leaving it open like a door. She picked up her phone and, before she could reconsider, called Kali, an actual call, voice instead of text, just to hear a real person answer. It rang twice. "Hey," Kali said. "Hey," Naomi said. "Fifty seconds and counting."

activity: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
knowledge_domain: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
fact: Principle 15 of the 1992 Rio Declaration states that where there are threats of serious or irreversible environmental damage, lack of full scientific certainty should not delay cost-effective preventive measures.
story:
The purple vest made Sadie a part of the hospital the way a costume makes anyone part of a play, and she had learned in four shifts that people would tell a teenager in a vest almost anything. Her job was simple: deliver water, restock the family lounge, wheel the cart of dog-eared magazines from room to room on the fourth floor. What she wanted tonight was harder to carry. On Monday her civics class had split in half over a proposed pesticide for the county's wheat fields, and Mr. Bui had made her the moderator, which meant she had to hold a position by Friday, and she had none yet.

Aikam had argued for waiting. "You can't ban a thing because it might be bad," he'd said, tapping his pen on the desk. "That's not evidence, that's fear." Ireland had fired back something about the precautionary principle, though she hadn't been able to say exactly what it was, and the argument had ended with Aikam calling her position unscientific and Ireland calling his amoral, both of them looking at Sadie as though she were the referee who would finally award the match.

The man in room 412 was maybe sixty, thin in the way that makes age hard to guess, and his hands moved restlessly over the blanket when she set the water down. His daughter, a tired woman in a canvas jacket, sat by the window. "You're too young to remember when they said the river was fine," the man said, not to Sadie exactly, but she was the one standing there. "Swim in it all summer, they said. Then the fish went belly-up." His daughter said, "Dad, they never proved it was the plant," and he said, "That's the whole point, isn't it," and turned his face toward the window.

Sadie restocked the lounge down the hall and thought about how the word proved was doing a strange amount of work in that room. The daughter wasn't wrong; the evidence had stayed equivocal for years, studies pointing in different directions, and nothing so mushy could absolve anyone of anything. Yet the fish were dead. She wondered whether causality had to be certain before you were allowed to act on it, or whether waiting for certainty was itself a decision, the same as any other.

On her break she texted Ireland: what is the precautionary principle actually, in words. Ireland sent back a photo of a page from an environmental law textbook she'd checked out of the library, and beneath it a line: "Principle 15 of the 1992 Rio Declaration." The photo said that where there are threats of serious or irreversible environmental damage, lack of full scientific certainty should not delay cost-effective preventive measures. Sadie read it three times. It wasn't a claim that the pesticide was harmful. It was a claim about who had to bear the waiting.

She carried that sentence back up to the fourth floor like something fragile in her pockets. On the way she passed the daughter in the hallway, on her phone, arguing with someone about whether to sign a consent form for a procedure the doctors had described as probably helpful. "Probably," the daughter kept saying. "They said probably." Sadie stood by the cart, not eavesdropping exactly, just standing, and noticed how the same word could be a comfort in one mouth and a trap in another.

In 412 the old man was asleep. Sadie left the water and took the empty cup, and the daughter looked up and said, "Sorry, you didn't need to hear all that." Sadie said it was fine, she was writing a paper on almost exactly this, except about wheat. "Well," the daughter said, "whoever gets hurt, I hope somebody's writing it down before it happens next time." She said it lightly, the way people say heavy things in hospitals, and went back to her phone.

Friday came, and Sadie stood at the front of the class and said she had started with Aikam's side, that evidence mattered, that you couldn't run a society on suspicion. Then she said the old man's name was nothing she knew, but the fish were dead, and Principle 15 said that where there are threats of serious or irreversible environmental damage, lack of full scientific certainty should not delay cost-effective preventive measures. Aikam raised his hand and asked who decided what counted as a threat, and Sadie said she didn't know, that this was the part she kept turning over, and Ireland leaned back in her chair and said, "So you're saying wait, but not too long." Sadie looked at her notes, at the single line she'd underlined twice. "I'm saying waiting is a choice too, and somebody pays for it either way."

"Then which way do we vote?" Aikam asked, and Sadie capped her pen.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The 2026 FIFA World Cup, hosted by Canada, Mexico and the United States, was the first with 48 teams and the first hosted by three countries.
story:
Loic's skates hung over his shoulder by the laces as he followed his father through the lobby of the rink, past the scoreboard that still showed last night's amateur score, 3 to 1, glowing over an empty sheet of ice. In the banquet room they had rented for the semifinal viewing party, his uncle was already arguing with Christopher about the format of the tournament, and Loic could hear it from the hallway.

"Thirty-two," Christopher said, arms crossed, wearing his club jersey indoors like armor. "It's always been thirty-two. It's tradition."

"You're remembering the old days," the uncle said, spreading cheese on a cracker with great confidence. "This one's bigger. Sixty."

"Forty," said Maddie, who was sitting cross-legged on the floor beside the projector cable, testing whether the picture would hold.

Loic set his skates down on a folded chair. He had read something about this, weeks ago, in an article he had half-absorbed while eating cereal, and now the detail surfaced the way a coin surfaces in shallow water. He let them go around twice more, because they were enjoying themselves, and because being right too quickly was a kind of rudeness.

"It's forty-eight," he said.

Three faces turned. His mother, arranging the sandwiches into rows, paused with the mustard knife in the air.

"Forty-eight teams," Loic said. "And it's not just one country hosting. It's three. Canada, Mexico, and the United States. First time for both things." He had not known the second part this morning; he had looked it up two days ago after his father claimed, over dinner, that the whole thing was in America. Loic had disabused him of that gently, with the phone held out like evidence in a small courtroom, and his father had said "huh" in the tone of a man revising a map in his head.

"Forty-eight," Christopher repeated, as though tasting a suspicious fruit. "That's a lot of teams nobody's heard of."

"That's the point," Maddie said. "More countries get to be in it. That's the whole argument, isn't it. Who it's for."

The projector flickered, steadied, and the stadium appeared, enormous and green, the crowd a single breathing thing. Loic's little cousin clapped at nothing in particular. The game began.

It was, for the first half, a nervous and friable affair, both teams attacking in ways that fell apart the moment they met resistance, passes shattering on the midfield like stale cake. Loic found himself thinking about the argument while watching the ball move, the way the tournament had been stretched wider to let more countries in, and how Christopher hated that because it diluted the thing, and how Maddie loved it because it widened the door, and how both of them were describing the same change with opposite words. He had always assumed there was a right answer to questions like that, the way there was a right answer to how many teams qualified. But the number was a fact and the question of whether the fact was good was not, and he could feel the difference between the two under his hands like the difference between ice and water.

At halftime his uncle tried to explain, to everyone at once, why expanded tournaments were ruining football, and Mr. Das, the neighbor from two doors down who had come because he liked the company more than the sport, said mildly, "I only came for the sandwiches," which made Loic's mother laugh so hard she had to sit down on the drinks table, which wobbled, which made everyone move very fast.

"Loic thinks more teams is good," Maddie announced, pinning him with it.

"I think it's good that more countries get to play," Loic said slowly. "I also think Christopher's right that some of the games will be worse. I don't know how to weigh that against each other yet." It came out less awkward than he expected. Nobody groaned. Christopher even nodded a little, the way you nod at an opponent who has stopped pretending.

The second half was better than the first, one team scoring twice in ten minutes, the second goal a long bending shot that made the whole banquet room rise off its chairs, even Mr. Das, who had said he was only there for the sandwiches. Loic shouted with everyone else and did not think about anything at all for a full minute, which was its own kind of answer, or at least its own kind of rest.

Afterward, when the room had emptied and his father was stacking chairs and Maddie was coiling the cable and the ice beyond the wall sat quiet and blank, waiting for the public skate, Christopher lingered by the door.

"Forty-eight," he said. "I'm going to look it up anyway."

"Look it up," Loic said. "Bring snacks."

Christopher grinned and pushed the door open into the cold.

activity: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
knowledge_domain: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
fact: Niger has one of the highest birth rates in the world, so its population pyramid has a very wide base and a large share of children.
story:
The travel agency sat between a dry cleaner and a shuttered phone repair shop, and on Saturdays it smelled of both. Kaitlyn had taken the job filing brochures because Ms. Mori paid cash and let her use the back table after closing, and because the geography assignment Ms. Mori had offered to help with was due Monday. The task was to compare two population pyramids and argue what each country would need more of in twenty years, schools or nursing homes.

Kaia arrived at four with a laptop and two iced teas, and Bruce came because his mother's salon was next door and he had nowhere else to go. They spread the printed pyramids across the table, over a stack of brochures for river cruises Ms. Mori had not yet shelved. One pyramid belonged to Japan. It bulged in the middle, wide at the ages above fifty, narrow at the bottom. The other belonged to Niger, and Kaitlyn turned it sideways to make sure she was reading it right. It looked like a steep triangle, almost a cliff of young people.

"So Niger builds nursing homes," Bruce said, pointing at the triangle, "because that's what a triangle means, right?"

Kaitlyn said she didn't think so. She slid the Japan chart toward him. Japan's shape was the one aging, the one that would fill care homes; the country had a large share of older people and comparatively few children coming up beneath them. Niger's chart was the opposite. It had a very wide base, and when she added up the bars for the youngest ages, a large share of the whole population was children. She had read a line in her textbook that morning and copied it into her notes: Niger had one of the highest birth rates in the world. The pyramid was what that looked like drawn as bars.

"Then it needs schools," Kaia said. "Like, a lot of schools."

"Classrooms now, and then jobs in fifteen years," Kaitlyn said, and pulled a brochure toward her to write on the back of it. The brochure advertised a river journey with a hotel Ms. Mori had described to a customer that morning as riparian, right on the water, with balconies facing the current. Kaitlyn turned it over and sketched two little pyramids in the margin of the Nile route map.

Bruce argued the other side anyway. He said that if you couldn't be sure what a government would do, you couldn't predict anything, and the whole assignment was a guess dressed up as analysis. Kaitlyn had been thinking about that since Tuesday, when she'd blamed the printer for a missing page and Ms. Mori had found the page in Kaitlyn's own binder. The printer was exculpated, Ms. Mori had said dryly, holding the sheet out to her, and Kaitlyn had gone home and looked the word up. The etymology had seemed obvious once she saw it: from the word for blame, meaning to clear of it. So she understood the appeal of finding something outside yourself to blame, or to trust. But Bruce was asking her to exculpate herself from the prediction entirely, and she didn't think that was honest.

"You can't know what they'll build," she said. "But you can know what the population is doing. The wide base isn't a guess. It's a count." She tapped the Niger chart. "Those bars are children who already exist. They'll need desks whether anyone plans for it or not. What stays uncertain is whether anyone plans for it."

Ms. Mori came out from the back with a box of brochures and looked over their shoulders. She said nothing about the pyramids, only that if they were going to write on her merchandise they could at least buy it. Kaia bought the riparian one, two dollars, and Kaitlyn kept her sketch.

They stayed until the streetlights came on. Kaia drafted the paragraph on Japan, Bruce grudgingly wrote the section on what a government could still get wrong, and Kaitlyn wrote the central claim in her own hand: Niger's pyramid, wide at the base, heavy with children, pointed toward schools. She left a sentence at the end acknowledging what she could not account for, then crossed it out, then wrote it again. On her way out she shelved the cruise brochures in the rack by the window, where the light caught the river on the cover, running the whole length of the page.

activity: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
knowledge_domain: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
fact: TinEye, a reverse image search engine launched in 2008, can sort results with the oldest first, helping find when an image first appeared online.
story:
Rose had shared the video before first period ended, and by lunch she regretted it. The clip showed a flooded street with cars floating sideways past a storefront, and someone had captioned it "downtown this morning." Her aunt lived downtown. So did Connor, which was why he found her at her locker, phone out, jaw tight.

"You sent me that flood thing," he said. "My mom's calling me in a panic because it's two blocks from her office."

"It said this morning."

"Rose." He turned his phone toward her. The same water, the same floating sedan, the same crooked sign, but the video was captioned in a different language and the timestamp read years earlier. He'd found it through TinEye, he said, and she should look herself before she told anyone else.

They sat on the floor outside the auxiliary gym, where the hallway was empty during lunch, and Rose opened her laptop. TinEye, he explained while she typed, was a reverse image search engine launched in 2008; you uploaded a picture and it found where else that picture lived online. She cropped a frame from the flood video and dropped it in. Hundreds of results scrolled past, the same street dressed in different headlines, different cities, different emergencies. Then she found the setting for sorting and chose oldest first. The earliest match surfaced at the bottom of the page, dated before she'd even started high school, posted on a small regional news site covering a storm that had happened somewhere she'd never heard of.

"That's it," she said. "That's the original. Everything else is a copy wearing a new caption."

"So you're going to send out a correction?"

She looked at the post she'd made that morning, her own words under the borrowed water: please share, people need to see this. Twenty-three people had. She thought about how easy it had been, one tap, how the shock of the image had desensitize her, in a way, to the question of whether it was true. The scarier a picture looked, the faster she wanted it out of her hands and into everyone else's. "I don't know if a correction fixes anything," she said. "The video's already moving faster than I am."

Bryce came around the corner with a bag of chips and dropped down beside them. "Mr. Rahman wants the media literacy pieces by Friday," he said. "I was going to write about how you shouldn't believe everything online. Very original, I know."

"That's not a piece," Rose said. "That's a fortune cookie." She was still staring at the search results, the image repeated and repeated like a rumor changing clothes. "This is the piece. One photo, five floods, and a tool that can tell you which flood came first."

She unposted her share that afternoon, then did something harder: she posted again, this time with the original date and a screenshot of the sorted results, oldest first. A few people liked it. Someone commented that the flood was still happening somewhere, so what did it matter. She let that sit for an hour before answering, because she wasn't sure it didn't matter, and she didn't want to pretend otherwise. What she wrote in the end was plain: the water was real, the drowning cars were real, but it wasn't our street and it wasn't this morning, and her aunt was fine.

Bryce knocked on the door of the school paper's office on Thursday, holding a printed draft. Mr. Rahman read it standing up, one hand on the filing cabinet. "There's a line here about the paper's indemnity," he said. "Where'd that come from?"

"Rose. She said if we publish other people's photos, we should be able to show we checked where they came from, otherwise the liability's on us."

Mr. Rahman read the page again, slower. "She said that."

"She also said you should keep the boring parts," Bryce said. "She said the boring parts are the proof."

Rose wasn't in the room to hear any of this. She was in the library with her laptop open, running a different flood photo through the search a second time, because the first pass had given her two possible originals and she wanted to be sure before she messaged her aunt's group chat. Down the table, Connor watched her flip between tabs, counting dates on his fingers.

"Same storm?" he asked.

"Different storm," she said. "Same year." She screenshotted both results, side by side, and hit send.

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
knowledge_domain: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
fact: Milk chocolate is usually tempered to a lower working temperature than dark chocolate, around 29-30 degrees Celsius, because milk fat softens the cocoa butter.
story:
Lucas arrived at the market before seven, when the vendors were still unfolding awnings and the gravel held the night's cold. Ms. De Vries had given him the corner of her stall, between the jars of honey and the buckets of dahlias, and a folding table with a marble slab on it. He was seventeen and had told everyone, including Maximilien and Guillaume, that he was learning to temper chocolate, and now he actually had to do it.

"You melted it in the double boiler?" Ms. De Vries asked. She was already weighing out honey sticks for the first customers.

"To forty-five. Then I cooled it on the slab, working it, and brought it back up." He showed her the thermometer clipped to the bowl. "Thirty-one and a half. That's where dark is supposed to be."

She nodded and went back to her customer, a woman buying three jars of buckwheat honey. Lucas dipped a knife into the bowl and laid a thin stripe of chocolate on the edge of the marble. He waited. In four minutes the stripe of dark chocolate he had done earlier had set hard, glossy under the awning's light, and when he bent the knife blade under it, it snapped. He had done that one at thirty-one and a half degrees, and it had worked.

He had also brought milk chocolate, because Maximilien had said the customers at a market would rather buy milk, that dark was for people who wanted to be seen buying dark. Lucas had thought about that for a while. He didn't want to commodify the difference between the two, selling one as an identity and the other as a default, but he also wanted to sell what people would actually buy, and those two thoughts did not sit easily together.

The milk chocolate, brought to the same thirty-one and a half, sat on the marble like wet paint. He drew a fingertip through the stripe from the earlier batch. It smeared. It had been twenty minutes and it still smeared, dull and soft, and when he lifted the edge it bent like a shoelace instead of snapping.

Guillaume turned up around eight with a coffee and his little sister's wagon, which he was supposed to be filling with vegetables. He watched Lucas lay another test stripe and watched it stay wet.

"Maybe your thermometer's broken," Guillaume said.

Lucas tested the dark again, from the same thermometer, same bowl method. It snapped. "It's not the thermometer."

"Maybe milk chocolate's just like that. Soft."

"It sets in bars. It snaps in bars. I've eaten enough of it." Lucas scraped the failed stripe back into the bowl. He had a card in his apron pocket, notes he'd copied from a book at the library, mostly about dark chocolate because the book assumed everyone started there. The milk chocolate section had been tangential, half a page near the end, and he had skipped it because the dark section had seemed like the real thing, the technique itself. He took the card out now and turned it over.

On the back, in his own handwriting from three days ago, was a line he had copied without thinking about it: milk chocolate is tempered lower than dark, around twenty-nine to thirty degrees, because milk fat softens the cocoa butter.

He read it twice. Twenty-nine to thirty. He had been working his milk at thirty-one and a half, dark chocolate temperature, and it would not set.

Guillaume leaned over his shoulder. "That says milk fat softens the cocoa butter. So it works lower."

"So it works lower," Lucas said.

He cooled the bowl on the marble, dragging and folding the chocolate until the thermometer read twenty-nine and a half, then held it there, nudging it back over the warm water a few degrees at a time. He laid a stripe on the marble and set the timer on his phone for four minutes and didn't watch it, because watching it wasn't going to change anything. He helped Ms. De Vries stack honey jars instead.

At four minutes the stripe was set. He slid the knife under the edge and pressed down. It snapped, and the surface caught the morning light in a way that looked manufactured, like something from a box, except that he had made it on a folding table at a farmers' market.

Ms. De Vries came over and looked at the stripe, then at the bowl, then at him. "So what did you learn?"

"Milk goes at twenty-nine, thirty. Dark goes higher." He turned the failed batch over in the bowl, still soft, and then looked at the snapped stripe. "I don't know if the card's rule is the whole rule, though. I got twenty-nine and a half to work. Whether thirty-one would have worked, or twenty-eight, I didn't test."

"Then test it next Saturday," she said, and put two honey jars in front of a customer.

activity: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
knowledge_domain: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
fact: A linear search checks items one by one from the start, so in the worst case, when the target is last or missing, it must look at every item.
story:
The attendance program had been crawling since second period, and by lunch Steve was convinced the network was dying. Eva leaned over his shoulder in the computer lab and watched the little spinner turn on the screen. Ms. Owusu had given them the school's old roster file as a dataset, two thousand names, and Steve's lookup script was supposed to find a student by name and print back their homeroom. It worked fine when he searched for Adaar, Bianca. It seized up completely when he searched for Vela, Ruth.

"It's not the network," Eva said. She pulled a chair over. "Watch. Search for someone at the top of the file, it's instant. Search for someone at the bottom, it takes forever. Search for someone who isn't there at all, it takes the longest."

Steve ran it three times to prove her wrong, and the evidence accumulated against him. Bianca came back in under a second. A name from the end of the file took long enough that he got up, filled a paper cup at the fountain down the hall, and came back still waiting. Then he typed in Zellweger, Marta, who had transferred away in September, and the spinner turned and turned while they ate half a bag of pretzels. "It's like it's mad at me," Steve said.

Charles-Edouard drifted over from the far terminals, because he always drifted over when something broke. He had spent the morning arguing in their politics thread that the school board was a miniature plutocracy, since the families who funded the robotics team decided which competitions got buses, and he was still in the mood to fight about systems. "Your problem isn't hardware," he said. "Look at your loop."

Eva read the code while Steve defended himself. It was a clean, honest little program: start at the first line, compare, move to the next, compare again. She counted on her fingers what it was actually doing. If the name was first, one check. If the name was last, two thousand checks. If the name wasn't anywhere, it checked all two thousand anyway and only then gave up, because a linear search checks items one by one from the start, so in the worst case, when the target is last or missing, it must look at every item. She said the last part out loud, slowly, testing it. "Linear search. That's what Ms. Owusu called it Monday."

"You weren't even listening Monday," Steve said. "You were drawing."

"I listen with half my brain. The other half draws." She was already flipping to the page in her notebook where she'd doodled through the lecture. There was a diagram she'd copied without understanding: a sorted list, with an arrow stabbing the middle. She'd thought it was a thermometer at the time. Now she saw it was a decision. The file was alphabetical, which suddenly seemed less like tidiness and more like an asset. "The list is sorted," she said. "We're searching it like it's a jumble of receipts."

Charles-Edouard caught on faster than either of them, because Charles-Edouard loved the idea of halving things, power cut in half, options cut in half. "You jump to the middle," he said. "If your name is past that point, you throw away the first half. Then the middle of what's left. Like a cosmopolitan guest at a party who only talks to whoever's actually interesting." Steve told him that analogy made no sense, and Charles-Edouard said analogies were how the plutocracy kept people from learning to code, which was a joke, mostly.

They rewrote the script together, Eva at the keyboard, the boys calling out boundary conditions she'd have missed alone. When it came time to test, she hesitated over Zellweger, Marta, the missing name, the one that had caused the whole afternoon. Steve noticed her pausing and slid the pretzels toward her, which was his way of saying go on. She typed it. The program jumped to the middle, threw away a thousand names, then five hundred, then smaller and smaller, and reported not found in less time than it took the cursor to blink. She ran Bianca, then the last name in the file, then Marta again, three times, because the missing case still felt like it ought to cost something.

Ms. Owusu stopped behind them on her way to the front of the lab and read the screen for a moment without saying anything. Eva started explaining, then stopped herself, because the printout was already explaining it, all four searches lined up with their times, the worst case now indistinguishable from the best. "We should write it up," she said instead, and pulled the notebook toward her, past the thermometer, to a clean page. At the bottom she added one line for herself, small, where the boys wouldn't tease her: still not sure why the original took so long to give up, only that it did, every time. Steve leaned over and read it anyway. "That's the whole point, though," he said. "It never knew when to stop looking."

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: India has marked voters' fingers with indelible ink based on silver nitrate since its 1962 general election, so no one can vote twice.
story:
The line at the polling station wrapped halfway around the elementary school, so Morgan crossed the street to the coffee shop to wait it out, because standing still in a crowd made her feel like she was wasting the morning twice. Mario was already at the corner table, stirring the same cup of coffee into a slow vortex, and Christina had claimed the chair by the window with her boots up on the rung.

"You actually came," Mario said. "I thought you were going to philosophize about civic duty from your bed."

"I proselytize in person or not at all," Morgan said, dropping her bag. "It's more honest."

Christina ordered a croissant and, being a shameless epicure about breakfast, ate it in small deliberate bites while describing the polling line as though it were a natural disaster she had survived. Morgan's phone buzzed while she was mid-sentence about absentee ballots. It was a photograph from her aunt in Mumbai, held up at arm's length, grinning, her index finger stained a deep violet that looked almost black in the light.

"She voted today," Morgan said, turning the screen around. "Look at that. They mark your finger with indelible ink over there."

"Indelible," Mario repeated, as if tasting the word. "Like, permanent."

"Silver nitrate. It doesn't wash off." Morgan scrolled up through the thread. "It started with the 1962 general election, she says, so nobody can vote twice. You show up, you vote, they stain you, and for days afterward everyone knows exactly what you did." She found herself oddly moved by it, the way her aunt held the finger up like a trophy, the whole hand a small flag.

"That's kind of beautiful," Christina said. "Here you get a sticker. Mine will be on my jacket until it peels."

"I didn't think you'd be the sentimental type about elections," Mario said. "You spent all of September arguing that one vote is statistically meaningless."

"I spent September arguing with myself," Morgan said. "It's different." She turned her cup slowly on its saucer. "My dad's side says voting is a debt you owe, whether or not it counts. My mom says optimism is just math with feelings. I've been trying to hold both of them at once, and honestly it's like carrying two full cups." She nodded at the counter, where a man was walking very carefully toward the door with a latte in each hand. "But my aunt stood in line for four hours to get one finger painted. So maybe the point isn't whether it tips anything. Maybe the point is the proof. Something you carry that says you were there."

"That's the most dangerous thing you've said all year," Mario said. "Next you'll be telling me the sticker is sacred."

"Stickers are deleterious to my dignity," Morgan said, "but yes."

They finished their drinks and walked back together. The line had shortened, and Mr. Wiśniewski, who taught chemistry at the high school and was volunteering as a poll worker, stood at the check-in table with a clipboard, greeting former students with an air of patient ceremony. When Morgan gave her name, he ran his finger down the column, then down a second column, then looked up with a small apologetic wince.

"You're registered, but this isn't your precinct. Your parents moved in the spring, I think. You're across town, at the library on Fowler."

Morgan stood very still. "The library on Fowler."

"Fowler's lovely," Christina offered. "They have a café."

Morgan looked at her phone, at the clock, at the four blocks between here and there, and felt the morning rearrange itself around an address she had never bothered to learn. Mario leaned against the doorframe with his hands in his pockets, wearing the expression of a man who had been handed a gift.

"Say it," Morgan said.

"I would never," Mario said. "I'm just noting, purely as an observer, that the girl who proselytizes about civic duty doesn't know where she lives."

Morgan shouldered her bag and pushed through the door. From behind her, in the doorway, Mario called out, "Want the sticker off mine? It's practically indelible."

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: Psychologists call it misattribution of arousal when a racing heart caused by fear or excitement is mistaken for attraction to the person nearby.
story:
Parker arrived at the mall eleven minutes early, which he decided was wrong, so he walked once around the fountain on the ground floor and then sat on the bench nearest the escalators, where the girl from his chemistry class, whom he was meeting, would see him being casual rather than waiting. His phone showed a picture he'd taken of the ticket kiosk: two lanes booked at the bowling alley on the third floor, an option he had chosen over a movie because a movie delimits the evening to silence in the dark, while bowling, he reasoned, gave them something to do with their hands.

Tate worked at the sporting goods store near the fountain and was on break, sitting on the opposite end of the same bench with a soda. When he saw Parker checking his phone for the fourth time, he came over.

"Who's the lucky one?" Tate asked, and Parker told him: a girl from third period, that they'd talked twice, once about the lab and once about nothing, and that she'd said yes when he asked, which had surprised him more than the asking had.

"Third period," Tate said. "So you barely know her."

"I know she's funny. I know she hates the mall, and she agreed to come anyway."

Tate shrugged, crushed the can, and went back inside. That was the extent of the coaching available.

She arrived at four minutes past the hour, carrying nothing, wearing a jacket that suggested she had dressed quickly. Her name was on the lane screen before they had finished deciding on shoes: her initials, then his, because the cashier had asked and Parker had answered too fast. The first game went to her by nineteen pins. Parker bowled badly in a way he recognized as bad, dropping his shoulder, rushing the approach, and he said so, and she said her father had taught her on a league and that she'd been bowling since she was eight, which accounted for the difference better than any theory about nerves.

The second game he won, narrowly, and by the tenth frame of the third they were even, which the alley's screen rendered in amber lights that neither of them could stop looking at. She bowled first: nine pins, then the corner pin, a spare. He needed at least a mark. His first ball took out seven, leaving the ten pin standing, and the whole approach, the walk, the swing, the release, happened in a silence that seemed to have been arranged by the alley itself, and the pin went down, and his heart was going hard enough that he could feel it in his throat.

They stood at the counter afterward, waiting for the printout of the scores, and she was laughing about something, the way his final ball had hung on the edge of the gutter before breaking in, and he noticed that his hands were not steady, and that the unsteadiness felt like more than competition.

"Can I tell you something weird?" he said. "When I was throwing that last ball, I couldn't tell if I was terrified or having the best time of my life. It felt exactly the same."

"That's not weird," she said. "My psych class covered it. Misattribution of arousal. When your heart is racing from fear or excitement, you can mistake it for being attracted to whoever's standing next to you."

"So this," Parker said, gesturing at the space between them, at the scoreboard, at his own pulse, "could be the bowling."

"Could be," she said. "That's the fun part. You don't get to know."

They took the escalators down to the food court. On the second floor, past a store that sold Scandinavian furniture and had a wall-sized photograph of a Norwegian fjord, grey water between steep green cliffs, she stopped and looked at it for a moment and said her grandmother lived near one, and Parker asked what that was like, and she said cold, and that you could hear the ferry from her grandmother's kitchen, a low horn twice a day. He filed the detail away with the others: funny, hates the mall, grandmother on a fjord.

At the food court they got pretzels and found a table near the fountain, the same fountain, he realized, where the evening had almost begun. Tate's shift must have ended, because he passed by with his jacket on, clocked the two of them, and gave Parker a thumbs-up so scathing in its irony that Parker had to look at the table to keep a straight face.

"So the arousal thing," Parker said, once Tate was gone. "If it's real, then half of what people call a spark at a horror movie or a roller coaster is just the movie."

"Or," she said, tearing her pretzel in half and handing him the larger piece without comment, "people put themselves in those places on purpose, because they can't tell the difference either, and they'd rather feel something and sort it out later than feel nothing and be sure."

Parker considered this while he ate. He thought about how he had chosen bowling over a movie, and whether the choosing had been strategy or accident, and how the jitter in his arms had not gone away even now, ten minutes after the last pin, when there was nothing left to win. He could not delimit the fear from the excitement, and she had told him, plainly and without cruelty, that he might never be able to. That did not feel like a bad answer. It felt like the question had simply been handed to him, warm, with salt on it.

"What are you doing next Saturday?" he asked.

She pulled her jacket tighter, looked at the fountain, and said, "There's a roller rink on Route Nine."

activity: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
knowledge_domain: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
fact: A 1990 follow-up of Mischel's preschoolers found that those who had waited longer for the second treat tended to have higher SAT scores as teenagers.
story:
The campus tour had been promising until the parent started talking. Nicole stood at the back of the group in the psychology building lobby, holding a free pen she had taken mostly out of spite, while a man in a golf shirt explained to anyone within range that he had read about a famous study. Preschoolers, he said, were left alone with a single treat and told that if they could hold out, they would get a second one. He spread his hands like a magician revealing a card. "A 1990 follow-up of those same kids found that the ones who waited longer for the second treat tended to have higher SAT scores as teenagers."

"So one afternoon with a marshmallow decides your whole life," said his daughter, who had the flat look of someone who had heard this before, at dinner, in the car, possibly at holidays.

"That is not what the study says," the father began, but the tour guide, sensing danger, moved everyone toward the neuroscience wing.

Nicole followed, but the thing snagged in her like a burr. Tiffany caught up with her near the brain-scan posters and bumped her shoulder. "You're doing the face."

"What face?"

"The face where you're eviscerating somebody in your head. It was the dad, right? The marshmallow dad."

"He's not wrong that the study exists," Nicole said. "I've actually read about it. I just don't know what he thinks it's for." She turned the pen over in her fingers. "He said it like it was a verdict. Like the four-year-olds who grabbed the treat should have just been issued their SAT scores right there."

Bridget materialized beside them with a bagel she had liberated from the refreshment table, an altruistic act of acquisition, she explained, since she intended to share, though the bagel was already half gone. "My cousin went here," she offered. "She said the open house lies about everything except the dining hall, which is worse than advertised."

They drifted into a lecture hall where a professor was demonstrating an eye tracker, and afterward, when the room thinned, Nicole found herself next to Mr. Das, her chemistry teacher, who was apparently here for a conference and wearing the same cardigan he wore to school, as though the hundred miles between home and this campus were merely decorative. He had seen her at the tour, he said. He had heard the marshmallow father too.

"You looked skeptical," he said. "Not dismissive. Skeptical."

"I kept thinking about this kid I babysit," Nicole said. "He's five. He can't wait for anything. He once ate a raw potato because dinner was taking too long." Tiffany made a sound into her jacket. "And I thought, okay, so according to that guy, he's already behind. Except he also taught himself all the planets' moons last month, because nobody would read him the book again. He waited for that. He just doesn't wait for potatoes."

Mr. Das nodded slowly, and she braced for the explanation, the speech, the adult pivot where he told her what the study really meant. Instead he said, "I once failed a student who could not wait one day to look at her exam results, and who is now doing her residency in Boston. The waiting is not the same in every room." Then he checked his watch and said something about a panel on accreditation, which was clearly a lie, and left her with it.

She found Tiffany and Bridget outside on the quad, where they had discovered that the fountain, advertised in every brochure as a tranquil gathering space, was actually a loud concrete bowl in which a tour group was taking turns photographing a golden retriever someone had brought. Nicole sat on the fountain's edge and took the pen out again. She had been carrying it the whole time, she realized, the way you carry a decision you haven't made.

"Here's my problem," she said. "Part of me thinks the study is comforting. Like, if waiting at four predicts something at seventeen, then I should just wait for everything. The deposit, the commit button, all of it. Wait and get the second treat." Bridget offered her the last corner of bagel as a counterpoint, and Nicole took it, which they both noted without saying anything. "But the other part thinks that's insane. One afternoon. I failed my driving test twice and then got a perfect score. Which of those afternoons am I?"

"The perfect one, obviously," said Tiffany. "If we're picking."

"Nobody's letting you pick," Nicole said, but she was almost laughing. She looked out across the quad at the tour group, at the retriever standing heroically in the fountain while everybody's parents aimed their phones, and she thought about the four-year-olds, both the ones who waited and the ones who did not, all of them now in their forties somewhere, unknowable. Then she took out her phone and opened the application portal, and held her thumb over the button, and looked at it for a long moment.

"Potato," she said to herself, and pressed it.

activity: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
knowledge_domain: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
