fact: Ignoring air resistance, a ball dropped from a table and a ball launched horizontally from the same height hit a level floor at the same time.
story:
Carter had failed the physics quiz on Tuesday, and by Thursday he had stopped pretending otherwise. He sat at the picnic table in his backyard with the textbook open to a page of projectile problems, each one a little diagram of a cannon or a cliff with arrows branching off it like antennae. The trouble was that he kept treating the motion as one thing, one arc, one feeling of a ball flying, when the book kept insisting it was two motions stapled together: sideways and down. His pencil had worn a grey smear across the page where he'd erased the same setup four times.

Kaya arrived first, cutting through the back gate without knocking because that was the arrangement between their families, and Meriem came a minute behind her, carrying a bag of oranges and her own copy of the problem set, which she claimed she'd finished. She had not. She was, in Carter's private taxonomy, the loquacious one of the three, capable of narrating an entire failed attempt at a problem before her pencil touched paper, and today she began by announcing that the numbers in problem four were hostile by design.

They worked badly for an hour. Then Kaya, who had been flicking a bottle cap across the table out of boredom, stopped mid-flick and said, "I don't get why the launch angle even matters. Once the thing leaves your hand, isn't it just falling either way?"

Meriem said that was obviously wrong, because a ball you throw hard travels further, so it must stay up longer. Kaya said further wasn't the same as longer. The argument went around twice and then hardened into a bet: a dropped ball versus a ball thrown sideways, same height, and they would kneel on the grass and listen for which one hit the picnic table's bench first.

They used two oranges, which Meriem regretted immediately because she'd been saving them. Carter set the rules. One orange held out over the bench and released, the other pushed off horizontally from the same height, his left hand and his right hand, his best attempt at simultaneity. Kaya crouched with her ear near the wood. Meriem insisted on a second listener and crouched on the other side, which meant the two of them were now face to face under the bench like children in a fort.

I still thought of it as one motion, honestly, even standing there with an orange in each hand. But the bet had made it a question with ears, and a question with ears gets answered. I said "ready," and dropped the one and shoved the other, and Kaya and Meriem both heard what they heard, which was one sound. They made me do it again. One sound, again, so close together that neither listener would commit to a gap. On the third try Meriem said, "They landed together. Same time. I'm not saying that because of the bet, I'm saying it because it's true."

So the sideways throw didn't hold the ball up at all. That was the piece I'd been missing. The horizontal launch, the angle, the speed, all of that belonged to how far the thing went, and the fall ran on its own clock underneath, the same clock as a plain dropped ball, and the arc I'd been staring at was just those two motions laid over each other. Ms. Popescu, our neighbour, put her head over the fence and asked whether we were sacrificing fruit to something, and Kaya told her we were doing physics. "Ah," Ms. Popescu said, as if that were worse, and went back to her tomatoes.

We went back to the problems, and the diagram that had defeated me all week finally came apart in my hands. Separate the velocity into components, let each one run its own equation, and then the two answers had to be subsumed back into a single answer, a single point where the ball would be. It worked, at least it worked twice, and on the third problem the numbers came out slightly wrong, and I couldn't tell whether I'd broken a rounding rule or whether the whole picture was still missing something I hadn't met yet. Kaya thought it was rounding. Meriem thought it was fate. I wrote a small question mark beside it, which felt more honest than either.

The oranges sat on the bench, bruised on one side each, and the sun had moved far enough that the shadow of the fence lay across the page. Meriem picked up the fallen one, weighed it in her palm, and said, "Same height, same time. I want that on the quiz." Carter slid the last orange toward her. "Eat it," he said. "It's earned more than we have."

activity: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
knowledge_domain: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
fact: A digital elevation model is a raster layer storing the ground height of each cell, which GIS uses to predict where water will flow and collect.
story:
Sebastian's laptop sat on the kitchen table between a bowl of cereal he was no longer eating and a printed map of the city that Ms. Côté, his neighbour across the hall, had slipped under his door with a sticky note reading "for the flood kid." He was the flood kid now, apparently, because he'd told her at the mailboxes that his geography project involved mapping which neighbourhoods would drown first. She had laughed so hard she'd dropped her flyers for the building's annual general meeting.

The problem was that the map disagreed with him. He had loaded the flood risk layer over the housing layer, exactly as the tutorial said, and the shading made no sense. streets right beside the river, the ones with the cute little waterfront benches, showed up pale green, barely risky at all. Meanwhile a grid of streets three kilometres inland, nowhere near any water, sat under a blotch of dark blue that meant high risk. He toggled the layers off and on as if the map might correct itself out of embarrassment.

Moses arrived at four with his backpack and zero invitation, which was their arrangement. He leaned over Sebastian's shoulder and said, "Your map's broken. Those streets are nowhere near the river. I've walked them, there's a laundromat."

"I know there's a laundromat."

"Unless the laundromat floods."

"Everything floods eventually if my map is right, which it isn't, which is the problem."

Moses dropped into the chair across the table and stole the cereal, which by then was pure grey mush, and even he abandoned it after one spoonful. Sebastian clicked through the tutorial again, then through the software's help panels, which had clearly been written by someone who thought "pan and zoom to your area of interest" counted as instruction. On the TV in the living room, muted, a documentary about the open ocean played, and a title card floated past about pelagic birds crossing whole hemispheres without landing, which Sebastian found, in his current mood, unbearably smug.

Gillian called at five because Tuesday was her night to demand progress reports. "Did you fix the ghost flood?" she asked. That was her name for it, and it stuck immediately, because naming things was what Gillian did; she had already tried to codify their whole project into a system of colour-coded tabs, which Sebastian had quietly ignored.

"The ghost flood lives," Sebastian said. "The river's fine. The laundromat's doomed. I don't get it."

"Maybe it's not about distance from the river," Gillian said, in the tone she used when she wanted credit for an idea she hadn't finished having. "Maybe it's about height. Like, where's lower."

Sebastian opened the list of layers in his project file. Beneath the housing layer and the flood layer sat a third, greyed out because he'd never turned it on, labeled DEM. He clicked it. The city reshaped itself into a wash of colour, each cell shaded by the height of the ground it covered, a relief portrait of a place he'd walked his whole life. The streets near the river, he saw at once, sat on a gentle rise. The laundromat's neighbourhood lay in a shallow bowl, low and flat, three kilometres from anything wet.

"It's a digital elevation model," Moses said, reading off the layer's description. "Raster layer. Stores the ground height of each cell." He said it in his game-show-announcer voice, and then, quieter, with real interest: "So that's how it predicts where water goes. The water doesn't care about the river. The water cares about downhill."

They spent the next hour chasing the water. Sebastian used the software's flow tools on the elevation layer and watched blue threads crawl across the city, collecting, gathering, pooling in exactly the dark blotch over the laundromat. The river's own floodplain spread out thin and harmless onto its raised banks. His two layers, which had seemed to be lying to each other, turned out to be in perfect agreement once he could see the ground between them. It felt less like solving the problem than like a small rapprochement between the river and the rain, who had apparently been in negotiation about that low bowl for centuries without consulting anyone's real estate agent.

He screenshotted everything and typed the caption "YOUR BENCHES ARE FINE, YOUR LAUNDROMAT IS DOOMED" before he could think better of it, and sent it to the group chat.

Ms. Côté knocked at seven with a plate of rice and beans, her standard currency for services not yet rendered. "Tell me, flood kid, am I safe on the fourth floor?"

"You're on the fourth floor of the only building in this neighbourhood that's actually on high ground," Sebastian said. "You're the safest person I know."

She accepted this with visible satisfaction, then paused at the door. "And the units in the basement across the courtyard? The ones the landlord keeps advertising as 'garden level'?"

Sebastian looked at his map, at the dark blue blotch sitting squarely over her building, on the low ground, in the bowl, three kilometres from the river.

"Garden level," he said. "You might want to mention the garden part at the annual general meeting."

"I already did," said Ms. Côté. "I quoted you."

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Social loafing, the drop in effort people make in groups, shrinks when each member's individual contribution can be identified.
story:
The park had two diamonds and one usable one, which meant the summer league softball team practiced on the outfield grass while a family reunion occupied the infield until sundown. Alexia arrived early because early was the only thing she could control. She had made this team by a margin of one error in the tryout scrimmage, and for three weeks she had watched herself, in games, become a slower, warier version of the girl who practiced. In practice she dove. In games she played it safe on the first bounce and hated herself for it, and then played it safe again.

Kenzie noticed, because Kenzie noticed everything and kept most of it. "You're guarding yourself out there," she said one Tuesday, lacing her cleats on the bench near the water fountain. "Like the ball costs money."

"Maybe it does. We're two and five." Alexia pulled her cap lower. "Everyone else coasts too. Did you see Dean jog to first on that popup in the fourth? He jogged. The shortstop dropped it and he was still out."

Kenzie didn't argue, which was its own kind of agreement. The whole team ran at practice speed, all thirteen of them, a loose herd circling the outfield fence while the coach read emails on his phone. Nobody was lazy exactly. It was more like effort dissolved when you poured it into a group, the way sugar disappeared into water and left everything tasting faintly the same.

The change came from Ms. Ross, who coached the team across the park and had, for reasons no one established, decided to interfere. She was maybe sixty, sun-cured, with a penurious little whistle she refused to replace even when it produced more air than sound. She walked over during their water break and asked Alexia, not the coach, whether the team tracked anything. Times. Reps. Anything at all.

"We track wins and losses," Alexia said. "Mostly losses."

"Then you're tracking the wrong unit." Ms. Ross looked at the outfield, where Dean was showing a younger kid how to choke up on the bat. "My grandmother worked in a textile mill. Twelve women at a table, one quota. When they started counting each woman's own output, the quota got beat. Same women, same machines." She drank from the fountain and left it at that, walking back toward her own players without a lecture, which Alexia later understood was the whole point of her.

That night Alexia looked it up, because she was eighteen and could not leave a loose thread alone. There was a name for it. She found the term in a used textbook's chapter on groups, read it twice, and then read the study it came from, in which rowers pulled harder alone than in crews, and in which the gap closed when each rower's pull was measured and shown. She sat with that for a while. It wasn't a character flaw, then, Dean's jog or her own safe bounce. It was something about being one of many, a shadow the group cast over each person inside it.

At the next practice she brought a clipboard. She had written everyone's name down the side and, across the top, the word sprints, and under it the only column she intended to fill at first. She stood at the fence with a borrowed stopwatch and called them in. "New thing," she said, when they gathered, suspicious, caps low against the four o'clock sun. "We're timing sprints. Individual times. Yours, not the team's."

Kenzie frowned. "Why?"

"Because effort drops in groups, and it drops less when each person's contribution can be identified. It's called social loafing." Alexia held up the clipboard so they could see the empty grid. "We've been loafing. All of us. Me included."

Dean laughed, but he was the first in line, and when he ran he ran the whole way, through the outfield grass and around the tetherball pole she'd set as the turn, and his time, 11.4 seconds handwritten where anyone could see it, made something shift in the loose herd. The second girl through beat her own expectation. By the fourth runner they were arguing about the stopwatch's accuracy, which was its own kind of caring. The coach looked up from his phone once, then put it in his pocket and stood behind Alexia, watching her write numbers down.

She kept the sheet all season. She was careful with it, because she could already see the failure modes: a slow kid humiliated, a fast kid smug, a team that started running for the clipboard instead of for each other. When the youngest player, a fifteen-year-old who had been terrified since tryouts, posted the worst time two practices running, Alexia left her column blank the third day and wrote only the improvement from her first recorded sprint, a margin of half a second, and circled it. She wasn't sure that was the right call. It was possible you couldn't make effort visible without also making rank visible, and possible that rank was the poison and visibility the cure, both at once, inseparable. The book didn't say. The book only said the direction the numbers moved.

They finished four and nine, which was not a turnaround, and Alexia didn't pretend it was. But in the last game, a loss by one run in extra innings, she went back on a ball she had no business reaching, laid out on the outfield grass with the scoreboard dark behind her, and came up with it in her glove, dirt in her teeth, the runner holding at second. From the fence, where Ms. Ross's team was packing up, she heard that thin broken whistle, once, and applause from the wrong sideline.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: During Diwali, celebrated by Hindus, Jains, Sikhs and some Buddhists, families light small oil lamps called diyas in homes and temples to symbolize light overcoming darkness.
story:
The temple hall smelled of ghee and marigolds, and Maya's arms ached from carrying trays of small clay lamps from the storeroom to the wide sill beneath the windows. Her aunt wanted five hundred of them set out in rows before the guests arrived at seven, and it was already half past five.

"You're placing them too close," her aunt said, kneeling beside her, adjusting a lamp by a centimetre as though a great deal depended on it. Maya did not argue. She had learned, over eighteen years of Diwali preparations, which battles were worth having, and the spacing of diyas was not one of them.

The real battle was in her pocket. Her phone held a message from Faisal, sent an hour ago: "Tommy got us on the guest list for the open mic at nine. Last one before everyone leaves for college. You in or not." She had read it four times while arranging lamps. The temple celebration would run late; her mother had already claimed the drive home; and Maya had promised, months ago, before any of it mattered, that she would be here.

She set out another row, wicks threaded, oil poured to the same depth in each. Her grandmother had told her once, when she was small and impatient, why they did this, that the lamps were called diyas and that families lit them in homes and temples during Diwali to show light overcoming darkness. Maya had accepted it then the way she accepted bedtime. Now the phrase circled back to her with an anachronistic weight, a promise made by people centuries dead to people not yet born, and she could not decide whether that made it more worth keeping or impossibly distant from her actual life.

Her uncle was at the far end of the hall, holding forth for two of the temple volunteers about the family's origins, as he did every year. He could expatiate for twenty minutes on their ancestors crossing the steppe, though Maya suspected half the geography was invented, a pasteboard ancestry assembled from pride and a few photographs. Tonight his voice slid over her. She was counting lamps.

Her reply to Faisal took three drafts. The first said yes. The second said no, family thing, sorry. The third, the one she sent, said: "Can't get there till late. Save me a seat if you can. If not I'll understand." She stared at it after sending, aware that she had written a message that committed her to nothing and cost her something anyway.

At six fifteen Mr. Visser arrived. He taught chemistry at her school and lived two streets from the temple, and though he was not of their faith he came each year, drawn by something he never quite named, carrying a box of candles that he said were "for the overflow, in case you run short." Maya's aunt greeted him with the particular warmth reserved for people who show up without being asked. He knelt beside Maya at the window sill.

"May I?" he said, gesturing at the tray. She slid it toward him. He lit nothing; he only placed, following her spacing exactly, and after a few minutes he asked, quietly, why lamps and not candles, why oil and not wax.

"They're called diyas," she said. "Families light them at Diwali, in homes and in temples, for light overcoming darkness." She heard herself say it and recognized her grandmother's cadence in her own voice, and did not know what to feel about that, so she placed another lamp.

"Who celebrates it?" he asked. "Just your community?"

"Hindus, Jains, Sikhs," she said. "Some Buddhists too." She had looked it up in ninth grade for a project and never forgotten, the way one remembers a fact that turns out to be larger than the assignment.

At seven the guests began arriving, and the diyas were lit one by one, her aunt working from the far end, Maya from the near, until the rows met in the middle and the whole sill glowed in low, wavering lines. Maya's mother found her there, phone still heavy in her pocket, unread.

"Tommy's thing?" her mother asked. Not accusing. Just asking.

"Tell me when we can leave," Maya said, "and I'll go or I won't, but I want to choose it, not just end up somewhere."

Her mother looked at her a long moment, then at the lit sill, then nodded once and moved off toward the kitchen. Maya stood between the window and the door, one side of her face warm with lamplight, and took out her phone. Faisal had replied: "Seat saved. Till midnight." She typed nothing yet. She watched a younger cousin, six years old, reach out one careful finger toward a flame, and her aunt, not stopping her, saying only, "Slow."

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: The world's first food bank, St. Mary's Food Bank in Phoenix, Arizona, was founded in 1967 by John van Hengel.
story:
The neighborhood cleanup had been Sloane's idea, the way most things were, and by ten o'clock the three of them had dragged a tangle of sogty cardboard and broken pallets from behind the chain-link fence of the old warehouse on Delmore Street. Jonathan had expected to spend the morning bagging litter. Instead a man in a lanyard came out, introduced himself as Mr. Bekele, and asked whether they knew what went on inside the building. When Joaquin said, facetious, "Storage for haunted furniture," Mr. Bekele only smiled and held the door.

Inside, the warehouse smelled of cardboard and cold concrete. Metal shelving ran to the ceiling, sorted into canned vegetables, pasta, diapers, infant formula. Mr. Bekele handed them aprons and put them at the sorting table with a flats of dented cans, and while Sloane was still tying her apron strings, Jonathan drifted toward the poster taped to the cinderblock wall. It was a printed history, faded at one corner, and he read it twice because the first line seemed too early to be real.

"The world's first food bank," he said aloud. "St. Mary's, in Phoenix, Arizona. 1967."

"Founded by a guy named John van Hengel," Sloane said, coming up behind him. She had read the same poster last summer, when she'd volunteered here for three weekends running, and she said it the way people recite things they half own.

Joaquin didn't look up from his cans. "So it's an American invention, like jazz and drive-throughs."

"Maybe don't joke yet," Sloane said. "Wait until you've been here longer than nine minutes."

Jonathan let it go, but the date stayed with him through the morning, working at his hands the way a splinter does. 1967. His parents had been children then. He tried to picture someone standing in a warehouse like this one, in a city he'd never seen, deciding that surplus food and hunger ought to meet in a building with shelves, and then everyone afterward copying the shape of the idea. He had assumed hunger was just a condition of the world, like weather. Apparently it had an architecture, and the architecture had a birthday.

The real work was slower and stranger than he'd imagined. Half the cans were unlabeled, and Mr. Bekele taught them the rule: anything swollen or leaking went out, anything doubtful went into a quarantine bin for staff to judge. Around eleven a woman came through the line with two small children, and Jonathan watched Sloane greet her by name and slide an extra box of granola bars into her cart without announcing it. When the woman left, he asked why she hadn't said anything.

"Because then it becomes a favor," Sloane said, "and favors get paid back."

He turned that over while he sorted. It seemed to him there were two ways to think about the whole place, and they didn't sit easily together. One was Sloane's way, quiet and particular, an extra box, a remembered name. The other was the poster's way: systems, scale, a man in 1967 inventing a machine that was still running in a neighborhood Jonathan had walked past a hundred times without once wondering what was inside. He had come that morning mostly because Sloane had asked, and because his college application wanted a service narrative, which he now felt a little ashamed of. He wanted to say some of this out loud, but every phrasing he drafted sounded like a speech.

At lunch, sitting on the loading dock with sandwiches from the donation cooler, Joaquin started in again. "Okay, but if you help people to feel good about yourself, is it even good? It's all just, like, whatever gets you through the night." He made a gesture that was supposed to encompass philosophy.

"That's relativism," Jonathan said, "and it's lazy, and you're using it to excuse yourself for standing around while we sorted four hundred cans." Joaquin began to expostulate, hands up, claiming a shoulder injury of entirely recent invention, and Sloane laughed so hard she had to set down her sandwich.

But later, when Mr. Bekele was showing Jonathan how to log the morning's weights into a spreadsheet, each line a family somewhere he would never meet, Jonathan said, "The poster says a man named John van Hengel started all of it in 1967. Did he know it would get this big?"

Mr. Bekele considered the question without hurrying. "He started it because somebody across town had food and somebody else didn't and the distance between them seemed fixable." Then he handed Jonathan the clipboard and went to help a driver with the ramp.

Jonathan stood there with the pen. He still didn't know whether the right thing was the extra box of granola bars or the spreadsheet, the one name remembered or the four hundred cans, and he suspected the answer was both, and that both was harder than either. Sloane appeared in the doorway with a stack of empty crates.

"You're on the afternoon line with me," she said. "The woman with the two kids comes back Thursdays, by the way. Her name's not on the poster."

activity: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
knowledge_domain: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
fact: Aristotle held that people are responsible for actions done voluntarily, and that actions done under force or through ignorance of the circumstances can be involuntary.
story:
Sierra set the table the way her mother liked, forks on the left, and slid into her chair before the potatoes went around. Her phone sat face down on the counter where she'd left it, still buzzing every few minutes, and she kept hearing it the way you keep hearing a smoke alarm.

"You're quiet," her father said, spooning out seconds for her brother before taking any himself.

"I passed something on." She watched the steam rise off her plate. "A thing about Maelle. At lunch yesterday I told Brendan that she'd been the one who reported the sophomore trip for drinking, and by last period the whole grade had it, and it wasn't her. It was a teacher who saw the photos."

Her mother put her knife down. "Does Maelle know?"

"She knows it wasn't her. She doesn't know it started with me." The potatoes went cold in front of her. "I didn't make it up. Somebody told me it was her, and I believed it, and I repeated it. So I'm trying to figure out how much of this is actually mine."

Her brother, twelve and delighted by trouble, opened his mouth, and her mother cajoled him into silence with the promise of the last of the garlic bread, which he accepted with the dignity of a small king.

"Mr. Girma gave us a reading last week," Sierra said. She'd taken a photo of the page; she pulled the phone over, thumbed past the notifications, and read aloud. "Aristotle held that people are responsible for actions done voluntarily, and that actions done under force or through ignorance of the circumstances can be involuntary." She looked up. "I didn't know the circumstances. I didn't know it wasn't her. Does that make it involuntary? Like it just happened through me?"

Her father turned his glass a quarter turn on the tablecloth. "Did you want to believe it?"

That was the question she'd been avoiding. There had been a small satisfaction in it, a week after Maelle had gotten the solo in chamber choir that Sierra had wanted, a feeling of information being currency and her being briefly rich. She had not checked. She could have texted Maelle, could have asked one question, and had not wanted the answer to be no.

"I think there's a difference between what you're responsible for and what you're to blame for," her mother said, reaching over to refill Sierra's water before she'd asked, which was the kind of thing that undid her. "Blame is about the apportionment of the past. Responsibility can be about what you do next."

"That sounds like something you'd cross-stitch." But Sierra wrote it on her napkin anyway, apportionment, and under it, next.

She was not sanguine about the plan she made while carrying plates to the sink. She would tell Maelle at school, first thing, before Maelle found out some other way, and she would not decorate it with excuses. She would say she repeated something false, that she hadn't verified it, that she was sorry, and that she'd already texted Brendan and four others to correct it. She'd typed and deleted the message to Maelle three times during dinner; the last version was two sentences. The uncertainty she couldn't get rid of was whether Aristotle's idea covered her case or not. She hadn't been forced. She'd been ignorant, but her ignorance had been, in some part, chosen, like leaving a door unlocked and being surprised by the cold.

In the hallway after she dried the last dish, her phone buzzed again and this time she looked. It was Brendan. She read it twice under the dim light of the hallway.

so weird about the Maelle thing. i looked it up bc it bugged me. the photos got sent to the teacher by someone using a fake account. nobody knows who. i know i told people it was maelle too, after you said it. i feel terrible.

Sierra stood there holding the phone. Brendan had believed her, the way she had believed the anonymous someone, and each link in the chain could claim ignorance of the circumstances, each one pointing backward at the last, all the way back to a fake account and nobody. She thought of Mr. Girma saying once that a chain of involuntary acts could still add up to a very voluntary wreckage.

She typed back: We both tell her tomorrow. Together, before first period.

She carried her phone into her room, set her alarm twenty minutes early, and opened a new message to Maelle that said only, Can I walk in with you tomorrow? There's something I need to tell you, and it should be me who says it. Then she lay in the dark listening for the buzz that would tell her whether Maelle would even answer.

activity: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
knowledge_domain: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
fact: In his 1975 book Discipline and Punish, Michel Foucault used Bentham's panopticon as a metaphor for how modern institutions control people through the possibility of constant observation.
story:
Ryder clocked in at four and found a new screen bolted beside the registers, smaller than a laptop, showing the checkout lanes from a camera he'd never noticed in the ceiling. The assistant manager said it was a loss-prevention system, that it watched for "shrink events," and that when the box in the corner turned red, he was supposed to call a supervisor before the customer left. "It learns," she said, tapping the screen. "It's very smart." Ryder thought about saying that learning and smart weren't the same thing, but he needed the shift.

By five he'd seen the box turn red four times. Each time the flagged customer was a teenager, and each time the teenager had paid. Alfred, restocking gum at the impulse rack, leaned over and looked. "It's watching the hoodies," he said. "Notice that? Old guy in the sweater vest walks out with an unpaid soda under his arm, nothing. Kid in a hoodie breathes wrong, we get an alarm."

"That's a pattern, not a person deciding," Ryder said. He didn't know what to do with that yet. He was eighteen and three weeks from moving into a dorm, and the store had just cut two of six lanes to make room for four self-checkout kiosks, so the remaining cashiers had become attendants who watched people ring up their own groceries. The store manager had stood in the break room and eulogized the old express lane, called it a victim of progress, which everyone understood to mean a joke and nobody laughed at.

Ms. Huang came in around seven. She had been his ninth-grade English teacher and still lived two streets over; she bought the same things, ricotta and lemons and whatever fruit was marked down. Ryder had helped her carry bags to her car once when it was raining, and she'd told him he asked better questions than most adults, which he had kept for three years like something in a pocket. Tonight she used the self-checkout, mis-scanned a bag of lemons twice, and the box beside his register turned red.

He stood there while the screen said REVIEW: UNVERIFIED ITEM, CUSTOMER. He could call a supervisor, and the supervisor would come stand at Ms. Huang's elbow and ask to see her receipt, in front of the line, under the camera. Or he could walk over and scan the lemons himself, the way he would have done before the screen existed, quietly, because the machine had never had to be quiet.

He walked over. "Lemons don't like the scale," he said. "They roll." She watched him re-scan the bag and said, "Thank you, Ryder," in the voice she used to use when someone in class said something worth writing on the board. He felt the camera on the back of his neck the whole time, and he did the right thing anyway, and he wasn't sure the right thing felt the way he'd expected, because the alarm had not stopped and neither had the watching. It had just stopped mattering for ninety seconds.

That night he texted Maina, who was in his ethics elective and liked to argue more than she liked to win. The school had announced it was putting monitoring software on the laptops, something that flagged "off-task behavior" during study hall, and Maina had been drafting an objection all week. Ryder told her about the lemons, and the hoodies, and the assistant manager calling the system smart.

"Ms. Huang got flagged," he wrote. "She taught us to annotate in the margins and this thing thinks she's stealing citrus."

Maina called him. She was pacing, he could hear it. "Okay, so Foucault," she said. "I found him for my paper. In his 1975 book, Discipline and Punish, he took Bentham's panopticon, the prison with the tower where one guard can see every cell, and used it as a metaphor for how modern institutions control people through the possibility of constant observation."

"That's the watchtower," Ryder said.

"That's the watchtower. And Principal Okafor says the software is just a teacher's glance,数字化 for the digital age, but a glance looks at you and then looks away. The tower never looks away. You can't see the guard, so you behave like he's always there." She paused. "The difference isn't the camera. It's whether it blinks."

Ryder lay on his bed with the phone against his ear and thought about the four teenagers, about Alfred's hoodies, about the fact that he had fixed the lemons and nothing else. "So what do we do," he said, "if the tower's already built? Write a letter? Quit jobs with cameras? That's not a plan, that's a hobby."

"I don't know," Maina said. "Maybe the point is that somebody has to keep being the person who walks over and scans the lemons, and somebody else has to keep asking why the alarm went off at all. Both. Even if it's not a plan." She was right that it wasn't a plan, and he was surprised by how much the admission steadied him, the way a true scale reading steadies a bag of lemons.

The next afternoon Ryder was scheduled for the kiosks. He taped a folded piece of paper inside his vest pocket where he could touch it: a list, three names, of everyone flagged since Monday, which he'd copied off the screen before his break. Ms. Huang's lemons. A boy with a hoodie and exact change. An old man who hadn't been flagged at all, but whom Ryder had watched, on his own, walk out with the soda.

When the box turned red at 4:40, he looked at it, then at the mother in front of him whose card had declined twice and whose baby was crying under duress of the fluorescent lights, and he printed the store's coupon for formula from the register nobody monitored, and slid it across without a word. The alarm kept flashing behind him, red and patient, for the whole seven minutes it took her bag to stop shaking.

activity: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
knowledge_domain: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
fact: In a definite integral the constant of integration cancels out, because it is added to both F(b) and F(a) and then subtracted away.
story:
Mackenzie spread the returned quiz flat on the library table so the red ink faced the ceiling, as though the light might change what it said. Minus two, next to her answer to the last problem, and beside the minus two a circled note in Mr. Farah's handwriting: the constant doesn't belong here. She had written plus C the way she wrote it on every other problem that week, out of a caution that felt almost moral, and now she sat in the school library during her free period trying to understand what she had done wrong, or whether she had done anything wrong at all.

Tavin dropped into the chair across from her with a carton of chocolate milk and his own quiz, which showed a perfect score and a smudge of grease near the corner. "You're still on that?" he said. "It's two marks."

"It's not the two marks." She turned the paper toward him. "Look where he took them. Not on the antiderivative, on the final answer. The definite one. I got the number right. He crossed out the number and rewrote it without the C, like the C made the right answer wrong."

Tavin leaned over it, chewing the straw. Down the aisle behind them, the librarian was wheeling a cart of returns, and somewhere near the fiction shelves a keyboard clicked in slow, melancholic intervals, one person hunting and pecking through a research assignment nobody had started early. Tavin said, "I never write the C on those. Honestly I don't think about why."

"That's the problem," Mackenzie said. "I write it and I don't think about why either. We're doing the same thing."

He wanted, she knew, to get to the vending machines before third period, because Rafael had promised to save him a spot in the line for the good pretzels, and because Tavin's whole method of surviving senior spring was to let small problems stay small. It was a kind of desensitization, she thought, the way he practiced it, and it worked for him, and it probably kept him saner than she was. But she had spent four years building a system in which you followed the rules you were given, you showed your work, you wrote plus C, and the system had just docked her for loyalty. She couldn't let it go until she knew which of her rules was false.

She pulled a fresh sheet and copied the problem. Find the area under the curve from a to b. She wrote out her steps from the quiz, the antiderivative first, and there, unexamined, she had appended her constant. Then the subtraction: F at the upper bound minus F at the lower bound. She wrote both lines out long, no shortcuts, and sat back.

"Oh," she said.

"What?"

"Look." She slid the sheet across. "When I plug in b, I add C. When I plug in a, I add C. Same C, both times. Then I subtract the second from the first, and it just cancels." She tapped the two places where the constant appeared, the upper evaluation and the lower one. "It's added to both and then subtracted away. It never gets to the answer. It cancels out of every definite integral."

Tavin frowned at the page, then at his own quiz, then at the clock. "So Mr. Farah was right."

"He was right and he never told us why. He just wrote it doesn't belong." She was already amending her notes in the margin, in pencil. "I think that's what bothers me. I've been treating math like a religion, like you follow the form and get saved, and Tavin treats it like nothing, and both of us are wrong in the same direction. The rules have reasons. You're allowed to ask for them." She paused. "Or some of them do. I still don't know why e is what it is."

"That's rationalism," Tavin said, standing, crumpling the milk carton. "My brother took a whole class on it. Everything has to have a reason or you can't sleep."

"It's not that everything has a reason. It's that when there is one, sitting right there, I want to see it before I memorize the rule." She looked down at her page, where the two Cs sat in their matching positions before the subtraction erased them, and felt the small, clean satisfaction of a thing she had checked herself. "Also I'm keeping the plus C on the indefinite ones. That part's still true."

"Sure," Tavin said, backing toward the doors. "Tell Rafael your constant cancelled, he'll be thrilled."

The librarian passed their table again, pausing a half second at Tavin's abandoned chair. Mackenzie drew a box around the two lines of the subtraction, then wrote, underneath, in small letters, so future her would find it: it cancels, every time, it cancels. Then she picked up her pencil and started the next problem, plugging in the upper bound first.

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: The Common Application, which lets US college applicants send one application to many schools, was founded in 1975 with 15 member colleges and now has more than 1,000 members.
story:
The mailbox at the end of Tyler's driveway had a dented door that stuck in humid weather, and today, in the flat gray of an April afternoon, he had to work it open with both hands. Inside were a water bill, a grocery flyer, and a thick envelope from Hollis College, the school an hour north where he had interviewed in February and where, he admitted to himself now, he actually wanted to go. He stood there holding it, the flag of the mailbox still raised and forgotten behind him.

"Open it," Bryce said from the curb, where he had been waiting on his bike for ten minutes without saying anything. "Or don't. But you have to open it eventually."

"I know that." Tyler turned the envelope over. His mother was inside on the couch, still convalescing from the surgery in March, and she had made him promise not to check the mail until she could be at the window. She was at the window now. He could see the curtain move.

Bryce had applied to eleven schools, all through the same website, and he had opinions about it. "The Common App is the only reason that was survivable," he said, leaning his bike against the fence. "It started in 1975 with fifteen member colleges. Now it's got more than a thousand. One application, all those schools. My cousin had to write everything out by hand back in the day."

"Randy only did three," Tyler said. "He said the form made it so easy it felt like cheating, so he made himself write extra essays anyway."

"Randy is a lunatic."

Mr. Traoré came down the sidewalk with his dog, an old beagle that stopped at every mailbox as if checking its own mail. He had taught philosophy at the high school for thirty years and lived four houses down, and he slowed when he saw the envelope. "That is a decision," he said. Not a question.

"Hollis," Tyler said. "If it's thick, it's good. That's what everybody says."

"Everybody also said the earth was flat," Mr. Traoré said, but gently. The beagle nosed at Tyler's shoe. "You know, when I was your age, I believed an acceptance letter would tell me who I was. It does not. It only tells you where you may go. The rest is ontology. What a thing is, not where it is."

Tyler looked at him. "That's the second time you've used that word on me."

"And it will keep being true." Mr. Traoré smiled and moved on, the beagle shuffling behind him, and Tyler was left with the envelope and the sullen sky beginning to spit rain, his shirt darkening at the shoulders.

He thought about the kitchen table in October, the laptop open, his mother beside him with her tea, listing schools while he filled in the same biographical facts once instead of twenty times. He had added Hollis almost as an afterthought, after the school his father favored, after the one with the scholarship that seemed too good. His father wanted the practical one, the sure job, the degree that converted cleanly into money. His mother wanted the place Tyler had lit up describing, the small classes, the professor who wrote back to his email about the archaeology program. Tyler had told them both what they wanted to hear and had not decided anything, not really, and now the envelope was going to decide for him or against him, and he understood, standing there, that he had wanted it to decide, that he had been letting forms and letters do the work of choosing.

The rain came harder. Bryce ducked under the maple. "I'll wait inside if you're just going to stand there," he said, but he didn't move.

Tyler tore the flap with his thumb. The letter was one page, and he read the first line twice because his eyes had gone strange. "Dear Tyler," and then the word admitted, sitting there in ordinary black type. He read it aloud, once, to Bryce, and once louder, toward the window, and the curtain pulled back and his mother's hand came up against the glass.

"Call your dad," she called through the screen door, her voice cracking. "And get inside, you're soaked."

"In a minute," Tyler said. He folded the letter along its crease and put it in his jacket, over his heart like people did in movies, except he actually did it. Bryce whooped and slapped the fence. Somewhere down the block the beagle barked once at nothing, and Tyler walked up the driveway, past the mailbox with its door still hanging open.
